note: mvmt-program's ANATOMY without the drill lists: name, Latin, region, system, what it does (action) and why it matters clinically (clinical, practitioner-only). Read by the viewer when it has no parent frame to ask; embedded in mvmt-program the parent answers from its live library instead.

structures.name: Temporomandibular Joint
structures.action: The jaw joint. It hinges for the first part of opening, then slides forward for the rest.
structures.clinical: Two joints that must work as a pair. Watch the chin midline on opening — a swing to one side that corrects is a disc catching; a swing that stays is a joint not sliding.

structures.name: TMJ Articular Disc
structures.action: A cartilage pad between the two bones that moves with the jaw as it opens.
structures.clinical: The click is usually the disc slipping and relocating. Painless clicking is common and not by itself a problem. A jaw that will not open past about 25 mm and has stopped clicking may be a disc stuck in front of the joint.

structures.name: Masseter
structures.action: The thick muscle at the angle of the jaw. Closes the jaw powerfully.
structures.clinical: The most commonly treated jaw muscle and the most reliably tender. Visible hypertrophy at the jaw angle is a strong clue to night clenching.

structures.name: Masseter, Superficial Part
structures.action: The outer, larger portion running down and back to the jaw angle.
structures.clinical: What you feel when someone clenches, and the part that visibly hypertrophies in night grinders.

structures.name: Masseter, Deep Part
structures.action: The smaller inner portion, running more vertically.
structures.clinical: Sits closer to the joint and refers into the ear. Deep ear pain with no ear findings is often this.

structures.name: Temporalis
structures.action: Fan-shaped muscle over the temple. Closes the jaw and draws it backward.
structures.clinical: Refers pain into the temple, the eyebrow and the upper teeth convincingly enough to be mistaken for a headache or a dental problem.

structures.name: Medial Pterygoid
structures.action: Runs on the inner side of the jaw angle, mirroring masseter. Closes the jaw and moves it to the opposite side.
structures.clinical: Not reachable from outside. Suspect it where opening is limited and masseter work keeps helping only briefly — it refers into the ear and the back of the mouth.

structures.name: Lateral Pterygoid
structures.action: Pulls the jaw forward and to the opposite side. Its upper part attaches directly to the joint disc.
structures.clinical: The only jaw muscle attaching to the disc, which makes it central to clicking and deviation. Provoked by resisted forward movement rather than by clenching.

structures.name: Lateral Pterygoid, Superior Head
structures.action: The smaller upper head, attaching to the joint disc and capsule.
structures.clinical: The only muscle attaching to the disc, which places it at the centre of clicking. Active during closing, not opening — the opposite of its lower partner.

structures.name: Lateral Pterygoid, Inferior Head
structures.action: The larger lower head, to the neck of the mandible.
structures.clinical: Pulls the jaw forward and to the opposite side. Its side-to-side imbalance produces deviation on opening.

structures.name: Digastric
structures.action: Two bellies joined by a tendon at the hyoid bone. Opens the jaw and lifts the hyoid.
structures.clinical: Palpable under the jaw and along the front of the throat. Often tender in clenchers and in anyone with a long-standing forward head position.

structures.name: Digastric, Anterior Belly
structures.action: From the inner surface of the chin back to the hyoid.
structures.clinical: Trigeminal supplied. Palpable under the chin and commonly tender in clenchers.

structures.name: Digastric, Posterior Belly
structures.action: From behind the ear forward to the hyoid.
structures.clinical: Facial nerve supplied — two bellies of one muscle with different nerve supplies, because they develop from different pharyngeal arches.

structures.name: Mylohyoid
structures.action: Forms the floor of the mouth. Lifts the hyoid and helps open the jaw.
structures.clinical: Works with the tongue during swallowing. Tongue-press work reaches it better than any stretch.

structures.name: Geniohyoid
structures.action: Runs from the chin to the hyoid bone, drawing the hyoid forward and up.
structures.clinical: Too deep to treat directly. Trained rather than released, through tongue and swallowing work.

structures.name: Stylohyoid
structures.action: Runs from just behind the ear down to the hyoid, lifting and drawing it backward.
structures.clinical: Deep and hard to isolate. Relevant in persistent throat or ear discomfort with no ear cause found.

structures.name: Sternohyoid
structures.action: Runs from the breastbone up to the hyoid, pulling it downward.
structures.clinical: The most accessible of the under-hyoid group. Often tight alongside a short SCM in forward head posture.

structures.name: Omohyoid
structures.action: Runs from the shoulder blade to the hyoid in two bellies with a tendon between them.
structures.clinical: The only hyoid muscle attaching to the shoulder blade, which makes it a genuine mechanical link between shoulder position and jaw position.

structures.name: Sternothyroid
structures.action: Runs from the breastbone to the voice box, drawing it downward.
structures.clinical: Rarely treated directly. Relevant in voice complaints and in a sensation of throat tightness.

structures.name: Thyrohyoid
structures.action: Short muscle between the voice box and the hyoid bone.
structures.clinical: Completes the chain from breastbone to hyoid. Worth knowing rather than treating.

structures.name: Hyoid Bone
structures.action: A horseshoe-shaped bone in the front of the throat. The only bone in the body that articulates with no other bone.
structures.clinical: Held in position entirely by muscle, above and below. Its resting height is a direct readout of the balance between those two groups, and it shifts with head posture.

structures.name: Mandible
structures.action: The lower jaw. The only moving bone of the skull.
structures.clinical: One bone, two joints — it cannot move on one side without the other side responding. That is why single-sided jaw problems produce symptoms on both.

structures.name: Occipitofrontalis
structures.action: Two muscle bellies, one at the forehead and one at the back of the skull, joined by a broad sheet across the top.
structures.clinical: The band across the scalp transmits tension front to back, which is why a tight suboccipital region shows up as forehead pressure.

structures.name: Platysma
structures.action: A thin sheet just under the skin from the chest and shoulder up to the jaw.
structures.clinical: Superficial enough to be missed on palpation because you press straight through it. Relevant after neck surgery, burns, or long-standing guarding.

structures.name: Sternocleidomastoid
structures.action: Turns the head to the opposite side and tips it toward the same shoulder.
structures.clinical: Prominent, easily provoked, and commonly guarded after whiplash. Reaches end range fast — never force it.

structures.name: Scalenes
structures.action: Side-bend the neck and lift the first two ribs during breathing.
structures.clinical: Often involved where neck tightness comes with symptoms into the arm — the brachial plexus passes between them.

structures.name: Upper Trapezius
structures.action: Lifts the shoulder blade and side-bends the neck.
structures.clinical: Rarely genuinely weak. Usually overworking because lower trapezius and serratus are not holding their end — treat the cause, not the ache.
structures.modelNote: Z-Anatomy inverts the trapezius part names — its ‘ascending part’ is anatomically the upper trapezius. The mapping here follows the geometry, not the source labels, so the highlighting is correct.

structures.name: Levator Scapulae
structures.action: Lifts the top corner of the shoulder blade and side-bends the neck.
structures.clinical: The ropey band people point to at the neck-shoulder angle. Stretching it fails unless the shoulder is anchored down.

structures.name: Suboccipitals
structures.action: Fine control of the head on the top two neck joints.
structures.clinical: Dense with position sensors, so dysfunction here disturbs head-position sense as much as movement. A common headache source.

structures.name: Deep Neck Flexors
structures.latin: mm. longus colli et longus capitis
structures.action: Hold the head balanced over the neck and support the front of the spine.
structures.clinical: The single most under-trained group in the neck. Fails early, and the superficial muscles take over — which is why the neck feels tight rather than weak.

structures.name: Splenius
structures.action: Extend the head and turn it to the same side.
structures.clinical: Works with the opposite sternocleidomastoid to rotate. Guarded together with it after neck injury.

structures.name: Semispinalis Capitis
structures.action: Extends the head and supports the back of the neck.
structures.clinical: The greater occipital nerve pierces it — a frequent contributor to headache at the back of the skull.

structures.name: Cervical Facet Joints
structures.action: Paired joints at the back of each level that steer and limit neck movement.
structures.clinical: Pain is typically one-sided and worse turning toward the painful side. Sustained end-range extension plus rotation is the position to avoid.

structures.name: Cervical Discs
structures.action: Shock absorbers between the neck vertebrae.
structures.clinical: Disc-driven pain typically worsens with sustained flexion and eases with retraction — screen with press-ups before prescribing flexion work.

structures.name: Cervical Vertebrae
structures.action: Seven bones carrying the head, with the top two built for rotation rather than weight.
structures.clinical: Around half of all neck rotation happens at C1-C2 alone. Test it in full flexion, which locks the levels below.

structures.name: First Rib
structures.action: The top rib, sitting under the collarbone where nerves and vessels pass into the arm.
structures.clinical: An elevated first rib narrows that passage. Suspect it where neck tightness comes with arm symptoms and scalene work keeps relapsing.

structures.name: Rectus Capitis Posterior Major
structures.action: Runs from the C2 spinous process to the skull. Extends the head and turns it to the same side.
structures.clinical: The largest of the four and the one you can most reliably find. Connects by a fibrous bridge to the covering of the spinal cord — a direct mechanical link between this muscle and the structures around the brainstem.

structures.name: Rectus Capitis Posterior Minor
structures.action: Runs from the back arch of C1 to the skull. Extends the head.
structures.clinical: Attaches directly to the covering of the spinal cord. Implicated in headache after whiplash, where its role appears to be as much sensory as mechanical.

structures.name: Obliquus Capitis Superior
structures.action: Runs from the C1 transverse process to the skull. Extends and side-bends the head.
structures.clinical: Forms the upper border of the small triangle where the vertebral artery runs. Deep work in this area warrants care and light pressure.

structures.name: Obliquus Capitis Inferior
structures.action: Runs from the C2 spinous process to the C1 transverse process. The only suboccipital that doesn't attach to the skull.
structures.clinical: The primary rotator of C1 on C2, which is where roughly half of all neck rotation happens. Restriction here shows up as lost rotation when tested in full flexion.

structures.name: Splenius Capitis
structures.action: Runs from the upper thoracic spine to the skull behind the ear. Extends the head and turns it to the same side.
structures.clinical: Pairs with the opposite sternocleidomastoid to produce rotation — the two work as a diagonal. Refers pain to the top of the head.

structures.name: Splenius Cervicis
structures.action: Runs from the upper thoracic spine to the upper neck transverse processes.
structures.clinical: Deeper and lower than splenius capitis. Refers pain into the back of the head and behind the eye, and can produce a stiff neck that resists rotation.

structures.name: Scalenus Anterior
structures.action: Runs from the mid-neck to the first rib. Bends the neck sideways and lifts the first rib in breathing.
structures.clinical: The brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass between this and the middle scalene. The narrowest point of the whole thoracic outlet, and the reason scalene tightness produces arm symptoms.

structures.name: Scalenus Medius
structures.action: The largest scalene, running to the first rib behind the nerve bundle.
structures.clinical: The dorsal scapular nerve pierces straight through it, which is why scalene tightness can produce a deep ache along the inner border of the shoulder blade.

structures.name: Scalenus Posterior
structures.action: The smallest scalene, running to the second rib.
structures.clinical: Attaches one rib lower than the others, so it's involved in upper rib mechanics rather than in the neurovascular narrowing. Frequently blended with the middle scalene.

structures.name: Deltoid
structures.action: Lifts the arm away from the body, forward and back.
structures.clinical: Takes over when the cuff cannot centre the joint. A shrugging, deltoid-dominant raise is the visible sign.

structures.name: Anterior Deltoid
structures.action: The front fibres, from the collarbone. Lift the arm forward.
structures.clinical: Dominant in anyone who presses and trains little else. Its tightness feeds the forward shoulder posture usually blamed on the pecs.

structures.name: Middle Deltoid
structures.action: The side fibres, from the acromion. Lift the arm out sideways.
structures.clinical: The part that takes over when supraspinatus fails. A shrugging raise is this working alone.

structures.name: Posterior Deltoid
structures.action: The rear fibres, from the scapular spine. Draw the arm back and rotate it outward.
structures.clinical: Weakest of the three in almost everyone, and the one that holds the shoulder back. Trains with rowing and face pulls, never with pressing.

structures.name: Supraspinatus
structures.action: Starts the arm moving away from the body and holds the humeral head down in the socket.
structures.clinical: The most commonly injured cuff tendon. Loads heavily in the first 30 degrees, which is why the full can raise stops at shoulder height.

structures.name: Infraspinatus
structures.action: Rotates the arm outward and holds the head of the humerus back in the socket.
structures.clinical: The main external rotator and the main brake on a throw or a serve. Trained far too heavy by almost everyone.

structures.name: Teres Minor
structures.action: Rotates the arm outward alongside infraspinatus.
structures.clinical: Small, and usually trained together with infraspinatus rather than separately.

structures.name: Subscapularis
structures.action: Rotates the arm inward and is the largest of the four cuff muscles.
structures.clinical: The forgotten cuff muscle — everyone trains external rotation and skips this. Sits on the front of the shoulder blade, so it is not directly palpable.

structures.name: Pectoralis Major
structures.action: Draws the arm forward and across the body.
structures.clinical: Shortens with desk posture, pulls the shoulders forward and caps overhead reach. Each of its three parts shortens differently — stretch at three heights.

structures.name: Pectoralis Major, Clavicular Head
structures.action: The upper fibres, from the collarbone.
structures.clinical: Reached with the elbow below shoulder height — the lowest of the three doorway positions.

structures.name: Pectoralis Major, Sternocostal Head
structures.action: The bulk of the muscle, from the breastbone and rib cartilages.
structures.clinical: What most people mean by pec. Reached with the elbow at shoulder height.

structures.name: Pectoralis Major, Abdominal Part
structures.action: The lowest fibres, from the abdominal fascia.
structures.clinical: Smallest and most often missed. Reached only with the elbow above shoulder height — which is why one doorway position leaves part of the muscle untouched.

structures.name: Pectoralis Minor
structures.action: Pulls the shoulder blade forward and down over the ribs.
structures.clinical: Short pec minor tips the shoulder blade forward and narrows the space nerves pass through. A frequent hidden driver of both shoulder and arm symptoms.

structures.name: Latissimus Dorsi
structures.action: Pulls the arm down and back and rotates it inward.
structures.clinical: A major and frequently missed limiter of overhead reach, routinely mistaken for a stiff shoulder joint. It also attaches to the pelvis, so it links shoulder and low back.

structures.name: Teres Major
structures.action: Draws the arm down and back with latissimus dorsi.
structures.clinical: Restricts overhead reach with the lats. Often the tender spot found at the back of the armpit.

structures.name: Middle Trapezius
structures.action: Draws the shoulder blades toward the spine.
structures.clinical: Endurance rather than strength is what fails here. Train it in long sets.

structures.name: Lower Trapezius
structures.action: Draws the shoulder blade down and rotates it upward for overhead reach.
structures.clinical: Sets the shoulder blade before the arm goes overhead. Weak in almost everyone with a desk job, and the direct counterpart to an overworking upper trapezius.
structures.modelNote: Z-Anatomy inverts the trapezius part names — its ‘ascending part’ is anatomically the upper trapezius. The mapping here follows the geometry, not the source labels, so the highlighting is correct.

structures.name: Rhomboids
structures.action: Draw the shoulder blades together and slightly upward.
structures.clinical: Where people feel the ache between the shoulder blades. Usually a length and endurance problem rather than a strength one.

structures.name: Serratus Anterior
structures.action: Holds the shoulder blade flat against the ribs and rotates it upward.
structures.clinical: The muscle that actually lets the arm reach overhead. When it fails the blade wings and the cuff absorbs the load instead.

structures.name: Biceps Long Head
structures.action: Runs through the shoulder joint in a groove at the front of the humerus.
structures.clinical: Pain at the front of the shoulder in overhead athletes often traces here rather than to the cuff. Provoked by resisted forward reach.

structures.name: Glenohumeral Joint
structures.action: Ball and shallow socket — the most mobile joint in the body.
structures.clinical: The shallow socket is why it moves further than any other joint and dislocates most easily. Stability is muscular, not bony.

structures.name: Acromioclavicular Joint
structures.action: Small joint at the top of the shoulder where the collarbone meets the shoulder blade.
structures.clinical: Point tenderness right on top, worse with reaching across the body. The cross-body stretch is also the provocation test — use it to screen before prescribing.

structures.name: Scapulothoracic Articulation
structures.action: Not a true joint — the shoulder blade gliding on the back of the ribcage.
structures.clinical: A stiff ribcage caps shoulder blade movement no matter how strong the muscles are. Ribs before blade, blade before arm.

structures.name: Scapula
structures.action: A floating bone suspended on muscle, with its only bony link to the trunk through the collarbone.
structures.clinical: Its resting position and its ability to rotate upward govern nearly everything the shoulder can do.

structures.name: Trapezius
structures.action: A large diamond-shaped muscle from the skull and spine to the shoulder blade and collarbone, with three parts pulling in different directions.
structures.clinical: Treated as one muscle and behaves as three. The upper part is almost never weak and almost always overworking; the lower part is almost always weak. Treating the tight part without training the weak one is why it comes back.
structures.modelNote: Z-Anatomy inverts the trapezius part names — its ‘ascending part’ is anatomically the upper trapezius. The mapping here follows the geometry, not the source labels, so the highlighting is correct.

structures.name: Subclavius
structures.action: A small muscle beneath the collarbone, drawing it down and forward.
structures.clinical: Occupies the narrow space between collarbone and first rib that the nerve bundle also passes through. Small, but positionally significant in thoracic outlet symptoms.

structures.name: Coracobrachialis
structures.action: Runs from the coracoid process to the middle of the humerus, drawing the arm forward and in.
structures.clinical: The musculocutaneous nerve pierces straight through it, making it a compression site in heavy overhead athletes. Palpable high in the armpit with the arm abducted.

structures.name: Subacromial Bursa
structures.action: A fluid sac between the bony arch above and the rotator cuff below, letting the cuff glide as the arm rises.
structures.clinical: The largest bursa in the body. Painful arc between roughly 60 and 120 degrees of elevation is the classic finding — pain that eases above that range points here rather than at the joint.

structures.name: Glenoid Labrum
structures.action: A rim of cartilage deepening the shallow shoulder socket.
structures.clinical: Deepens the socket by roughly half and anchors the long head of biceps at its top. Tears there produce deep clicking or catching with overhead loading rather than a painful arc.

structures.name: Sternoclavicular Joint
structures.action: Where the collarbone meets the breastbone. The only true joint connecting the arm to the trunk.
structures.clinical: Everything the shoulder blade does passes through this one small joint. Easily palpated, rarely examined, and a real source of anterior chest pain that gets attributed elsewhere.

structures.name: Scapulothoracic Bursae
structures.action: Fluid spaces between the shoulder blade and the ribs allowing it to glide.
structures.clinical: Where snapping scapula comes from — audible or palpable grinding as the blade moves over the ribs. Usually mechanical rather than inflammatory, and it responds to serratus and posture work.

structures.name: Common Extensor Origin
structures.action: Shared attachment of the wrist extensors at the outer elbow.
structures.clinical: Tennis elbow. Isometrics first, eccentrics second — loading it early beats resting it, but the dose has to be right.

structures.name: Common Flexor Origin
structures.action: Shared attachment of the wrist flexors at the inner elbow.
structures.clinical: Golfer's elbow. Same principle as the outer side, and the ulnar nerve sits right behind it — screen for nerve symptoms before loading.

structures.name: Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis
structures.action: Extends the wrist and is the primary tendon involved in tennis elbow.
structures.clinical: The specific tendon at fault in most lateral elbow pain. Loads most with the elbow straight — which is why gripping with a straight arm hurts most.

structures.name: Wrist Flexors
structures.action: Bend the wrist and fingers, and contribute to grip.
structures.clinical: Short flexors reduce the wrist extension needed to bear weight through the hand — check before prescribing any floor work.

structures.name: Biceps Brachii
structures.action: Bends the elbow and turns the palm upward.
structures.clinical: The strongest forearm supinator. Loss of full elbow straightening after injury is often biceps guarding rather than a joint block.

structures.name: Biceps, Short Head
structures.action: Arises from the coracoid alongside coracobrachialis.
structures.clinical: Unlike the long head it does not pass through the joint, so it is not a source of front-of-shoulder pain. That is the point of separating them.

structures.name: Triceps Brachii
structures.action: Straightens the elbow; its long head also crosses the shoulder.
structures.clinical: Because the long head crosses both joints, a tight triceps limits overhead reach as well as elbow bend.

structures.name: Triceps, Long Head
structures.action: Arises from the scapula, crossing both shoulder and elbow.
structures.clinical: The only head crossing the shoulder, so it limits overhead reach when tight and must be tested with the arm overhead.

structures.name: Triceps, Lateral Head
structures.action: The outer head, from the humerus above the radial groove.
structures.clinical: Most visible and strongest in extension. Sits directly over the radial nerve's spiral course.

structures.name: Triceps, Medial Head
structures.action: The deep head, beneath the other two.
structures.clinical: Active through every degree of extension where the others assist at higher loads. The workhorse, and unpalpable through the others.

structures.name: Brachioradialis
structures.action: Bends the elbow, strongest with the thumb pointing up.
structures.clinical: Frequently tender in anyone doing repetitive gripping with a neutral forearm — hammering, racquet sports, manual therapy itself.

structures.name: Pronator Teres
structures.action: Turns the palm downward.
structures.clinical: The median nerve passes between its two heads — a compression site that mimics carpal tunnel but with forearm symptoms too.

structures.name: Pronator Teres, Humeral Head
structures.action: The larger superficial head, from the medial epicondyle.
structures.clinical: The median nerve passes between this and the deep head — the compression in pronator syndrome.

structures.name: Pronator Teres, Ulnar Head
structures.action: The smaller deep head, from the coronoid process.
structures.clinical: Forms the deep wall of the median nerve's passage. Absent in a small number of people.

structures.name: Carpal Tunnel
structures.action: Passage at the front of the wrist carrying the median nerve and finger flexor tendons.
structures.clinical: Symptoms in the thumb, index and middle fingers, typically worse at night. Glide the nerve, do not stretch it — and check the neck and pronator teres before assuming the wrist.

structures.name: First Dorsal Compartment
structures.action: Sheath at the thumb side of the wrist carrying the thumb's long tendons.
structures.clinical: De Quervain's. Extremely common in new parents from repeated lifting with the thumb out. Provokes easily — go gently.

structures.name: Elbow Joint
structures.action: Hinge for bending, plus a rotating joint at the radial head for turning the forearm.
structures.clinical: The last few degrees of straightening are the first thing lost and the hardest to get back. Time under a light load beats forcing.

structures.name: Flexor Carpi Radialis
structures.action: Bends the wrist and tilts the hand toward the thumb side.
structures.clinical: One of the main contributors to golfer's elbow through the shared inner-elbow tendon. Its own tendon is a prominent cord at the front of the wrist and a useful landmark.

structures.name: Flexor Carpi Ulnaris
structures.action: Bends the wrist and tilts the hand toward the little-finger side.
structures.clinical: The ulnar nerve runs between its two heads at the elbow, so a tight or overworked FCU is a genuine compression site. Treating the elbow flexor mass matters as much as treating the nerve.

structures.name: Flexor Carpi Ulnaris, Humeral Head
structures.latin: caput humerale m. flexoris carpi ulnaris
structures.action: From the medial epicondyle, part of the common flexor origin.
structures.clinical: The ulnar nerve enters the forearm between this and the ulnar head. That arch is the cubital tunnel's distal edge.

structures.name: Flexor Carpi Ulnaris, Ulnar Head
structures.latin: caput ulnare m. flexoris carpi ulnaris
structures.action: From the olecranon and the border of the ulna.
structures.clinical: The other wall of the nerve's entry. Tightness narrows the tunnel with elbow flexion.

structures.name: Palmaris Longus
structures.action: A thin muscle running to the palm, tensioning the palmar fascia.
structures.clinical: Absent in roughly one person in seven, on one or both sides — so a missing tendon is a normal variant, not a finding. Because it is expendable it is the usual tendon-graft donor.

structures.name: Flexor Digitorum Superficialis
structures.action: Bends the middle joint of the fingers.
structures.clinical: Each finger carries two flexor tendons; this is the superficial one and it splits to let the deep tendon pass through. That crossing point is where trigger finger catches.

structures.name: Flexor Digitorum Superficialis, Humero-ulnar Head
structures.latin: caput humero-ulnare m. flexoris digitorum superficialis
structures.action: The larger head, from the medial epicondyle and coronoid process.
structures.clinical: With the radial head it forms a fibrous arch the median nerve passes under — a further compression site distal to pronator teres.

structures.name: Flexor Digitorum Superficialis, Radial Head
structures.latin: caput radiale m. flexoris digitorum superficialis
structures.action: The smaller head, from the anterior border of the radius.
structures.clinical: Completes the arch over the median nerve. The two heads together define that passage.

structures.name: Flexor Digitorum Profundus
structures.action: Bends the fingertip joints. The only muscle that can.
structures.clinical: Split supply — median nerve to the index and middle fingers, ulnar to the ring and little. That split is why an ulnar nerve problem weakens the grip of only the last two fingers.

structures.name: Flexor Pollicis Longus
structures.action: Bends the tip of the thumb.
structures.clinical: The only muscle that bends the thumb tip. Loss of that movement with an intact grip is a specific sign of a median nerve problem above the wrist rather than at the carpal tunnel.

structures.name: Pronator Quadratus
structures.action: Deep square muscle joining the two forearm bones just above the wrist. The primary muscle that turns the palm down.
structures.clinical: Does most of the pronation work; pronator teres only assists under load. Sits directly on the interosseous membrane, so it is involved after distal forearm fractures.

structures.name: Brachialis
structures.action: Lies under the biceps and bends the elbow. The true workhorse of elbow flexion.
structures.clinical: Works regardless of forearm position, unlike biceps. Pain blamed on the biceps in front of the elbow is very often brachialis — palpate either side of the biceps tendon, not on it.

structures.name: Extensor Carpi Radialis Longus
structures.action: Straightens the wrist and tilts the hand toward the thumb. Attaches above the elbow rather than at the shared tendon.
structures.clinical: Because it attaches higher, it loads most with the elbow bent — which is why some people with tennis elbow hurt more carrying a bag than gripping with a straight arm.

structures.name: Extensor Digitorum
structures.action: Straightens the fingers at the knuckles.
structures.clinical: Its tendons are linked across the back of the hand, which is why lifting the ring finger alone is difficult. Loss of finger extension with intact wrist extension points at the radial nerve below the elbow.

structures.name: Extensor Digiti Minimi
structures.action: Independently straightens the little finger.
structures.clinical: Gives the little finger extension that does not depend on the shared tendon linkage. Minor on its own, useful for distinguishing a tendon problem from a nerve one.

structures.name: Extensor Carpi Ulnaris
structures.action: Straightens the wrist and tilts the hand toward the little-finger side.
structures.clinical: Its tendon sits in a groove that can snap in and out as the forearm rotates — a painful click on the little-finger side of the wrist with supination. Common in racquet sports and a frequent cause of ulnar wrist pain.

structures.name: Extensor Carpi Ulnaris, Humeral Head
structures.latin: caput humerale m. extensoris carpi ulnaris
structures.action: From the lateral epicondyle, part of the common extensor origin.
structures.clinical: Contributes to lateral elbow pain alongside the more commonly blamed ECRB.

structures.name: Extensor Carpi Ulnaris, Ulnar Head
structures.latin: caput ulnare m. extensoris carpi ulnaris
structures.action: From the posterior border of the ulna.
structures.clinical: Its tendon runs in the groove where subluxation produces the painful click on the little-finger side of the wrist.

structures.name: Extensor Indicis
structures.action: Independently straightens the index finger.
structures.clinical: Allows pointing without lifting the other fingers. Frequently harvested as a tendon transfer when the thumb extensor ruptures.

structures.name: Extensor Pollicis Longus
structures.action: Straightens the tip of the thumb and lifts it back away from the palm.
structures.clinical: Its tendon hooks around a bony ridge on the back of the wrist, where its blood supply is poor. Rupture weeks to months after a wrist fracture is a known and easily missed complication — inability to lift the thumb off a flat table is the test.

structures.name: Anconeus
structures.action: Small triangular muscle at the back of the elbow that assists extension and steadies the joint.
structures.clinical: Sits directly over the outer elbow, so it is frequently tender in tennis elbow and mistaken for the extensor origin. Palpate slightly behind and below the epicondyle to tell them apart.

structures.name: Supinator
structures.action: Wraps around the upper forearm and turns the palm upward.
structures.clinical: The deep branch of the radial nerve passes straight through it. That makes it a compression site producing outer-elbow pain that mimics tennis elbow but sits a few centimetres further down and does not respond to tendon loading. Worth testing before adding more load.

structures.name: Thenar Group
structures.action: The muscular bulge at the base of the thumb. Moves the thumb across the palm to meet the fingers.
structures.clinical: Median nerve supplied. Visible flattening of this bulge is a late and serious sign of carpal tunnel syndrome — by then the nerve has been compressed a long time.

structures.name: Hypothenar Group
structures.action: The bulge at the base of the little finger, moving and cupping that side of the hand.
structures.clinical: Ulnar nerve supplied. Wasting here alongside a normal thumb bulge separates an ulnar problem from a median one at a glance.

structures.name: Adductor Pollicis
structures.action: Draws the thumb in toward the palm. The main muscle of a key pinch.
structures.clinical: Ulnar supplied. When it is weak the thumb tip bends to compensate during a pinch — the thumb buckling while gripping paper is a classic ulnar nerve sign.

structures.name: Lumbricals of the Hand
structures.action: Four small muscles that bend the knuckles while straightening the finger joints beyond them.
structures.clinical: Produce the L-shaped finger position that a stiff or swollen hand loses first. No amount of gripping trains them — the position has to be trained directly.

structures.name: Interossei of the Hand
structures.action: Spread and close the fingers, and assist the lumbricals in the L-shaped position.
structures.clinical: All ulnar supplied. Hollowing of the web space between thumb and index is the earliest visible sign of ulnar nerve trouble and is easy to spot by comparing hands.

structures.name: Proximal Radioulnar Joint
structures.action: Where the radius head spins inside a ring of ligament at the elbow, allowing the forearm to rotate.
structures.clinical: Held by the annular ligament. In young children a sharp pull on the arm slips the radius head out of that ring — the classic pulled elbow, which reduces easily and is not a fracture.

structures.name: Distal Radioulnar Joint
structures.action: Where the two forearm bones meet at the wrist, completing forearm rotation.
structures.clinical: Cushioned by a cartilage complex on the little-finger side. Ulnar wrist pain worse with rotation and gripping, particularly after a fall onto an outstretched hand, points here.

structures.name: Interosseous Membrane
structures.action: A fibrous sheet between the two forearm bones that transfers load between them.
structures.clinical: Load through the hand is shared between radius and ulna via this sheet. When it tears alongside a radial head fracture the ulna migrates upward — a combination that turns a simple fracture into a difficult one.

structures.name: Flexor Retinaculum
structures.action: A tough band across the front of the wrist forming the roof of the carpal tunnel.
structures.clinical: The tunnel cannot expand — the floor is bone and the roof is this band. Anything that increases the contents, including swelling and fluid retention, raises pressure on the nerve. That is why symptoms are worst at night.

structures.name: Extensor Retinaculum
structures.action: A band across the back of the wrist holding the extensor tendons down, divided into six compartments.
structures.clinical: Each compartment can inflame separately. The first, on the thumb side, is de Quervain's; the sixth, on the little-finger side, is the ECU tendon. Knowing which compartment is tender names the problem.

structures.name: Palmar Aponeurosis
structures.action: A triangular sheet of fascia across the palm, protecting what runs beneath it and anchoring the skin for grip.
structures.clinical: Where Dupuytren's contracture forms — painless cords and nodules that gradually pull the ring and little fingers into the palm. Stretching does not reverse it, but keeping the palm mobile is worth doing early.

structures.name: Guyon's Canal
structures.action: A small tunnel on the little-finger side of the wrist carrying the ulnar nerve into the hand.
structures.clinical: Distinguishes itself from cubital tunnel by what it spares — the back of the hand keeps normal sensation, because that branch leaves the nerve before the wrist. Classic in cyclists from handlebar pressure.

structures.name: Cubital Tunnel
structures.action: The groove behind the inner elbow where the ulnar nerve passes, roofed by a fibrous band.
structures.clinical: The tunnel narrows as the elbow bends, which is why symptoms come on during phone calls and on waking with a bent arm. Numbness covering both the front and back of the little finger side places the problem here rather than at the wrist.

structures.name: Wrist Joint Complex
structures.action: Two rows of small bones giving the wrist movement in every direction.
structures.clinical: Weight-bearing through the hand needs roughly 70 degrees of extension. Most desk-bound people are well short and load the joint at end range instead.

structures.name: Thoracic Multifidus
structures.action: Small deep muscles crossing two or three levels, controlling movement segment by segment.
structures.clinical: Provides local control rather than gross movement. Segmental work reaches it; global extension does not.

structures.name: Thoracic Facet Joints
structures.action: Oriented to favour rotation, which is why the upper back is the body's main rotation engine.
structures.clinical: When these stiffen, the lumbar spine supplies the rotation instead — and it is not built for it. The most consequential stiffness in the body.

structures.name: Costovertebral Joints
structures.action: Where each rib meets the spine — they move with every breath.
structures.clinical: Sharp, well-localised back pain that catches on a deep breath usually sits here. Breathing work reaches it better than stretching does.

structures.name: Ribs
structures.action: Twelve pairs forming the ribcage, moving with breathing.
structures.clinical: Ribcage expansion caps upper back rotation. If the ribs do not move, rotation work has a ceiling no amount of stretching will lift.

structures.name: Diaphragm
structures.action: The primary breathing muscle, and part of the pressure system that stabilises the trunk.
structures.clinical: Breathing and trunk stability share the same muscle. Someone breathing through their neck is not going to brace well, whatever core work you give them.

structures.name: Intercostals
structures.action: Between the ribs, controlling their movement during breathing.
structures.clinical: Restriction here limits both breathing depth and trunk rotation. Side-bending with a long exhale reaches them best.

structures.name: Thoracic Vertebrae
structures.action: Twelve bones, each anchored to a pair of ribs, forming the least mobile part of the spine.
structures.clinical: The cervicothoracic junction at the top is usually the stiffest point and the true cause of many complaints blamed on the neck.

structures.name: Thoracolumbar Junction
structures.action: Where the rotating upper back meets the non-rotating lower back at T12-L1.
structures.clinical: A transition point and therefore a concentration point for load. Frequently symptomatic in rotational athletes.

structures.name: Serratus Posterior
structures.action: Thin sheets under the shoulder blade assisting rib movement in breathing.
structures.clinical: Often the source of a deep ache under the shoulder blade that resists surface work because it sits beneath the blade.

structures.name: Serratus Posterior Superior
structures.action: A thin sheet under the shoulder blade lifting the upper ribs during breathing in.
structures.clinical: A frequent source of deep ache under the shoulder blade that resists surface work, because the shoulder blade sits over it. Breathing work reaches it better than pressure does.

structures.name: Serratus Posterior Inferior
structures.action: Draws the lower ribs down and back during breathing out.
structures.clinical: Sits at the thoracolumbar junction and blends with the thoracolumbar fascia — one of the several structures that make that junction a concentration point for load.

structures.name: Sternum
structures.action: The breastbone. Three parts — manubrium, body and xiphoid process — anchoring the ribs at the front.
structures.clinical: The ridge where the top two parts meet sits level with the second rib, which makes it the landmark for counting ribs. It also sits at the level of the T4 and T5 disc behind.

structures.name: Costal Cartilages
structures.action: Cartilage bars connecting the ribs to the breastbone, giving the chest wall its spring.
structures.clinical: Costochondritis is tenderness at these junctions reproduced by pressing, and it is a common cause of chest pain that alarms people considerably. Reproducible on palpation is the reassuring feature.

structures.name: Lumbar Multifidus
structures.action: Small deep muscles controlling one or two segments at a time.
structures.clinical: Measurably shrinks within days of a back injury and does not recover on its own once pain settles. Segmental control work reaches it; deadlifts do not.

structures.name: Quadratus Lumborum
structures.action: Hikes the hip, side-bends the trunk, and steadies the twelfth rib for breathing.
structures.clinical: The classic one-sided low back ache in people who stand on one leg, carry a child on one hip, or sit twisted. Side plank work is the answer more often than stretching.

structures.name: Psoas Major
structures.action: Lifts the thigh and attaches directly to every lumbar vertebra.
structures.clinical: Filed under lumbar rather than hip because it attaches to the spine — a short psoas pulls the low back into extension. It also fatigues into the arched-back posture at the end of a long day.

structures.name: Transversus Abdominis
structures.action: The deepest abdominal layer, wrapping the trunk like a corset and raising internal pressure.
structures.clinical: Timing matters more than strength — it should fire fractionally before a limb moves, and after injury it fires late. Train the timing, not the crunch.

structures.name: Obliques
structures.latin: mm. obliquus externus et internus abdominis
structures.action: Rotate and side-bend the trunk, and resist both.
structures.clinical: In a rotational athlete their main job is resisting rotation, not producing it. Anti-rotation work loads them harder than any twisting exercise.

structures.name: Rectus Abdominis
structures.action: Bends the trunk forward and resists the back arching.
structures.clinical: Its useful role is anti-extension — holding the ribs down under load — rather than curling up. That is what the serve position and the overhead press demand.

structures.name: Thoracolumbar Fascia
structures.action: Broad sheet across the low back linking the lats above to the glutes below.
structures.clinical: The mechanical link between opposite shoulder and hip. Explains why a shoulder problem shows up as low back stiffness and the reverse.

structures.name: Lumbar Facet Joints
structures.action: Oriented to permit bending and block rotation.
structures.clinical: Pain worse with extension and rotation, easier with flexion — the opposite pattern to a disc. Loads hard in the kick serve and the overhead position.

structures.name: Lumbar Discs
structures.action: Shock absorbers between the lumbar vertebrae.
structures.clinical: Typically worse sitting and bending, easier standing and walking, worst first thing in the morning. Screen the direction of preference before prescribing anything.

structures.name: Sacroiliac Joint
structures.action: Where the spine meets the pelvis. Very little movement — its job is transferring load between trunk and legs.
structures.clinical: Pain typically pointed to with one finger just below the belt line. Usually a load-transfer problem, so single leg strength work beats mobilisation.

structures.name: Pelvic Floor
structures.action: Forms the base of the abdominal pressure system and works with the diaphragm on every breath.
structures.clinical: Part of the same canister as the diaphragm and transversus abdominis. Breath-holding through effort is a sign the system is not coordinating — and it belongs in any low back conversation, including with men.

structures.name: External Oblique
structures.action: The outermost abdominal layer, fibres running down and forward. Rotates the trunk to the opposite side.
structures.clinical: Works with the internal oblique of the other side as a diagonal pair — that pairing is the trunk's rotational engine and why anti-rotation work loads both.

structures.name: Internal Oblique
structures.action: Lies beneath the external oblique with fibres running the opposite way. Rotates the trunk to the same side.
structures.clinical: Its deepest fibres blend with transversus abdominis and behave like it, contributing to trunk pressure rather than rotation.

structures.name: Psoas Minor
structures.action: A small muscle in front of psoas major running to the pelvic brim, tilting the pelvis backward slightly.
structures.clinical: Absent in roughly four people in ten. Its absence is a normal variant and its presence contributes little, but it explains occasional anatomical confusion on imaging.

structures.name: Linea Alba
structures.action: The fibrous midline seam where the abdominal sheets from both sides meet.
structures.clinical: Where the abdominal wall separates in diastasis recti. The width matters less than whether tension can be generated across it — a wide gap that stiffens under load is a better outcome than a narrow one that domes.

structures.name: Rectus Sheath
structures.action: The fibrous envelope formed by the flat abdominal muscles wrapping around rectus abdominis.
structures.clinical: Its composition changes below a line partway down the abdomen, leaving the back wall of the sheath deficient below that point. That transition is a recognised site of abdominal wall pain and hernia.

structures.name: Iliolumbar Ligament
structures.action: Runs from the L4 and L5 transverse processes to the back of the pelvis.
structures.clinical: The main passive restraint on the lowest lumbar segment. A frequent and specific source of one-sided low back pain just above the pelvic rim, and easily confused with the sacroiliac joint below it.
structures.modelNote: The model draws this ligament’s iliac end about 1 cm above the top of the iliac crest, so it appears to float rather than attach. Its true attachment is on the inner lip of the crest, just anterior to the PSIS.

structures.name: Erector Spinae
structures.action: Three vertical columns running the length of the back. Extend the spine and control the descent into forward bending.
structures.clinical: Almost always overworking rather than weak — it stays switched on because the deep segmental system isn't doing its job. Works eccentrically far more than concentrically: it controls the lowering, it doesn't drive the lift.

structures.name: Iliocostalis
structures.action: The outermost column, attaching to the ribs. Extends and side-bends the spine.
structures.clinical: The column you reach first, running just lateral to the others along the rib angles. Side-bending work loads it more specifically than extension does.

structures.name: Longissimus
structures.action: The middle and longest column, running from the pelvis to the skull.
structures.clinical: The bulk of the erector mass either side of the spine. Its reach to the skull is why low back tension and neck tension so often travel together.

structures.name: Spinalis
structures.action: The innermost and smallest column, running close to the spinous processes.
structures.clinical: Thin, variable, and often poorly defined in the lumbar spine. Palpating it as distinct from longissimus is harder than textbooks suggest.

structures.name: Iliocostalis Lumborum
structures.action: Runs from the pelvis to the lower ribs.
structures.clinical: The thickest part of the lumbar erector mass and a frequent site of one-sided low back tightness in people who stand or carry asymmetrically.

structures.name: Iliocostalis Thoracis
structures.action: Runs between the lower and upper ribs.
structures.clinical: Works with breathing as well as posture, since it attaches only to ribs. Tender in people who brace or breathe shallowly.

structures.name: Iliocostalis Cervicis
structures.action: Runs from the upper ribs to the lower neck.
structures.clinical: Sits deep to the upper trapezius at the neck-shoulder junction. Frequently part of what feels like a stubborn trapezius that won't release.

structures.name: Longissimus Thoracis
structures.action: The largest part of the erector spinae, running from the pelvis and lumbar spine up through the thorax.
structures.clinical: The single biggest contributor to the erector mass you palpate either side of the spine. What most people mean when they say their back is tight.

structures.name: Longissimus Cervicis
structures.action: Runs from the upper thoracic spine to the neck vertebrae.
structures.clinical: Extends and side-bends the lower neck. Loaded constantly by a forward head position.

structures.name: Longissimus Capitis
structures.action: Runs all the way to the mastoid process behind the ear.
structures.clinical: Attaches to the skull alongside the sternocleidomastoid, so the two work as a pair. Involved in headache referral from the neck.

structures.name: Spinalis Thoracis
structures.action: Runs close to the spinous processes in the mid and upper back.
structures.clinical: The best-defined part of the spinalis column. Sits immediately either side of the bony bumps you can feel down the middle of the back.

structures.name: Spinalis Cervicis
structures.action: Runs between the upper thoracic and neck spinous processes.
structures.clinical: Small and variable, and absent in some people. Worth knowing rather than targeting.

structures.name: Spinalis Capitis
structures.action: Blends with semispinalis capitis at the back of the skull.
structures.clinical: So intimately blended with semispinalis capitis that they are usually treated as one. Listed for completeness rather than as a separate target.

structures.name: Transversospinalis Group
structures.action: The deep layer beneath erector spinae. Short muscles running diagonally from one vertebra up to another, controlling the spine segment by segment.
structures.clinical: Control rather than power. The deeper and shorter the muscle, the more it senses position and the less it produces movement — which is why this layer responds to slow segmental work and not to loading.

structures.name: Semispinalis
structures.action: The most superficial and longest of the deep layer, crossing four to six segments.
structures.clinical: Long enough to act as an extensor rather than purely a controller. Its cervical portion is substantial and often mistaken for erector spinae.

structures.name: Semispinalis Cervicis
structures.action: Runs from the upper thoracic transverse processes to the neck spinous processes.
structures.clinical: A major deep neck extensor, and the main muscular counterweight to a forward head. Wastes measurably in long-standing neck pain.

structures.name: Semispinalis Thoracis
structures.action: Crosses the mid and upper thoracic segments diagonally.
structures.clinical: Thin and variable. Contributes more to segmental control than to overall extension.

structures.name: Multifidus
structures.action: Crosses two to four segments. Thickest and most developed in the lumbar spine.
structures.clinical: Measurably shrinks within days of a back injury and does not recover on its own once pain settles. That's the single most useful fact about it — the tightness is not the problem, the wasting is.

structures.name: Cervical Multifidus
structures.action: The deepest layer at the back of the neck, crossing two to four segments.
structures.clinical: The deep neck extensors' equivalent of the deep neck flexors, and just as neglected. Both need training in neck pain, not just the flexors everyone remembers.

structures.name: Rotatores
structures.action: The deepest and shortest of the group, crossing one or two segments only. Best developed in the thoracic spine.
structures.clinical: Densely packed with position sensors — several times more than a limb muscle of the same size. Their job is telling the brain where each segment sits, more than producing rotation.

structures.name: Interspinales
structures.action: Tiny paired muscles between adjacent spinous processes.
structures.clinical: Too small to produce meaningful movement. Their density of position sensors suggests they exist to report segmental position rather than to change it.

structures.name: Intertransversarii
structures.action: Small muscles between adjacent transverse processes, assisting side-bending.
structures.clinical: Same story — sensors more than movers. Best developed in the neck and lumbar spine, where segmental control matters most.

structures.name: Levatores Costarum
structures.action: Fan-shaped muscles from the transverse processes down to the rib below. Lift the ribs.
structures.clinical: Sit right over the costovertebral joints, so they're frequently involved in the sharp, well-localised mid-back pain that catches on a deep breath.

structures.name: Gluteus Maximus
structures.action: Extends the hip and rotates it outward. The largest muscle in the body.
structures.clinical: Strong in almost everyone, poorly recruited in many. If the hamstrings cramp during bridging, it is not firing.

structures.name: Gluteus Medius
structures.action: Holds the pelvis level when standing on one leg.
structures.clinical: The single most important muscle for single leg control. Its failure shows as a dropping pelvis or a knee falling inward — and it shows on the stance leg, not the moving one.

structures.name: Gluteus Minimus
structures.action: Works with gluteus medius to steady the pelvis and rotate the hip inward.
structures.clinical: Refers pain down the outside of the leg convincingly enough to be mistaken for sciatica.

structures.name: Tensor Fasciae Latae
structures.action: Bends and abducts the hip, and tensions the IT band.
structures.clinical: Takes over abduction when gluteus medius is weak. Persistent TFL tightness is usually a symptom, not the problem — train the glute rather than stretching this.

structures.name: Iliotibial Band
structures.action: Thick fascial band from the pelvis to just below the knee.
structures.clinical: It does not meaningfully lengthen — it is not a stretchable structure. Symptoms come from compression at the knee under poor hip control, so treat the hip.

structures.name: Piriformis
structures.action: Rotates the hip outward with the leg straight, and inward once the hip is bent past 90 degrees.
structures.clinical: The sciatic nerve runs beneath it, and through it in a minority of people. Buttock pain with leg symptoms — test the nerve before deciding it is the muscle.

structures.name: Deep External Rotators
structures.action: Small deep muscles steering hip rotation and holding the head of the femur in the socket.
structures.clinical: The hip's equivalent of the rotator cuff. Rarely trained directly, and limited internal rotation usually traces here.

structures.name: Adductor Longus & Brevis
structures.action: Draw the leg toward the midline and assist hip flexion.
structures.clinical: Adductor longus is the most commonly strained groin muscle in change-of-direction sport. Copenhagen work is the strongest protection and is almost universally skipped.

structures.name: Adductor Magnus
structures.action: The largest adductor. Its rear portion functions as a hip extensor alongside the hamstrings.
structures.clinical: Effectively a fourth hamstring. Contributes significantly to hip extension power and is frequently missed in hamstring rehab.

structures.name: Gracilis
structures.action: Long thin adductor crossing both hip and knee.
structures.clinical: Crossing two joints means knee position changes its length — test adduction with the knee both bent and straight.

structures.name: Iliacus
structures.action: Lines the inner pelvis and joins psoas to lift the thigh.
structures.clinical: Unlike psoas it does not attach to the spine, so it affects hip position without directly pulling on the low back.

structures.name: Rectus Femoris
structures.action: The only quadriceps head crossing the hip as well as the knee.
structures.clinical: Because it crosses both, it must be tested with the hip extended and knee bent together. A tight rectus femoris tips the pelvis forward and is frequently misread as a low back problem.

structures.name: Hamstring Origin
structures.action: Common attachment of the hamstrings at the sitting bone.
structures.clinical: High hamstring tendinopathy — deep buttock pain, worse sitting on a hard chair and worse with stretching. Stretch it and it gets worse; load it and it improves.

structures.name: Hip Joint & Labrum
structures.action: Deep ball and socket, built for stability under load.
structures.clinical: Deep front-of-groin pain with a pinch at end-range flexion and internal rotation. Limited internal rotation is the earliest sign — measure it every visit.

structures.name: Pubic Symphysis
structures.action: The cartilage joint at the front of the pelvis.
structures.clinical: Loads where the two sides of the pelvis move asymmetrically — kicking, lunging, or late pregnancy. Adductor and deep abdominal work together, not either alone.

structures.name: Obturator Internus
structures.action: Arises inside the pelvis and turns sharply through a notch in the bone to reach the femur.
structures.clinical: The largest of the group and the one most worth knowing. Because it passes through the lesser sciatic notch it is a genuine site of deep buttock pain, and it can be reached internally when external work fails.

structures.name: Obturator Externus
structures.action: Covers the outer surface of the hole in the front of the pelvis and rotates the hip outward.
structures.clinical: Deep, anterior, and effectively unpalpable. Relevant in deep groin pain that does not behave like an adductor problem.

structures.name: Superior Gemellus
structures.action: A small muscle above obturator internus, blending with its tendon.
structures.clinical: Functionally part of obturator internus rather than independent. Named separately, treated together.

structures.name: Inferior Gemellus
structures.action: A small muscle below obturator internus, blending with its tendon.
structures.clinical: Same story as its partner above — part of the obturator internus complex in practice.

structures.name: Quadratus Femoris
structures.action: The lowest and squarest of the group, running from the sitting bone to the back of the femur.
structures.clinical: Sits in a narrow space between the sitting bone and the femur. That space narrows with hip extension and adduction, producing a deep buttock ache on walking that is easily mistaken for a hamstring origin problem.

structures.name: Adductor Longus
structures.action: The most superficial and most anterior adductor, forming a visible cord in the groin.
structures.clinical: The single most commonly strained groin muscle in change-of-direction sport, almost always at its attachment to the pubic bone. Palpable as a distinct cord with the hip abducted.

structures.name: Adductor Brevis
structures.action: Lies behind adductor longus, running from the pubis to the upper femur.
structures.clinical: The obturator nerve splits around it, one branch in front and one behind — which makes it directly relevant to obturator nerve entrapment in athletes.

structures.name: Sartorius
structures.action: The longest muscle in the body. Runs diagonally across the thigh, bending the hip and knee and turning the hip outward.
structures.clinical: Produces the cross-legged sitting position, which is where its name comes from. Contributes to the pes anserinus at the inner knee, so it links a hip complaint to inner knee pain.

structures.name: Pectineus
structures.action: A short flat muscle high in the groin that both bends and adducts the hip.
structures.clinical: Sits between the hip flexors and the adductors and behaves like both, which is why high groin pain often does not sort cleanly into either category. Frequently the tender point in deep anterior groin pain.

structures.name: Trochanteric Bursa
structures.action: A fluid sac between the bony point of the hip and the tendons crossing it.
structures.clinical: Lateral hip pain is now usually understood as tendon rather than bursa — gluteal tendinopathy, not bursitis. That matters because the treatment inverts: loading rather than resting, and avoiding the crossed-leg and hip-hitched positions that compress it.

structures.name: Iliofemoral Ligament
structures.action: A thick Y-shaped band across the front of the hip. The strongest ligament in the body.
structures.clinical: It is what stops you falling backwards when standing still — hip extension is checked by ligament, not muscle. Tight, it limits the hip extension a stride needs and the low back supplies the difference.

structures.name: Sacrotuberous Ligament
structures.action: Runs from the sacrum to the sitting bone, resisting the sacrum tipping forward.
structures.clinical: Blends with the hamstring origin and the thoracolumbar fascia, making it a direct mechanical link between hamstring tension and sacroiliac loading. Tender on deep palpation medial to the sitting bone.

structures.name: Sacrospinous Ligament
structures.action: Runs from the sacrum to the bony spine of the ischium, dividing the sciatic notch into two openings.
structures.clinical: It is what turns one notch into two — the sciatic nerve leaves above it, other structures below. Its position defines the anatomy of deep buttock pain.

structures.name: Inguinal Ligament
structures.action: A thickened band of abdominal fascia running from the front of the pelvis to the pubic bone.
structures.clinical: Everything entering the thigh passes under it — femoral nerve, artery, vein, and the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve. It is the reason a tight belt produces burning on the outer thigh.

structures.name: Adductor Canal
structures.action: A tunnel in the middle third of the inner thigh carrying the femoral vessels and the saphenous nerve toward the knee.
structures.clinical: Where the saphenous nerve is compressed, producing inner knee pain with no joint findings. Roofed by a fascial band under sartorius, so sartorius tension is part of the picture.

structures.name: Quadriceps
structures.action: Straighten the knee and control the descent of every step down.
structures.clinical: Switches off remarkably fast after knee swelling — within days. Reawakening it with quad sets comes before anything else.

structures.name: Vastus Medialis Oblique
structures.action: The inner fibres of the quadriceps that steady the kneecap in its groove.
structures.clinical: Cannot be trained in isolation despite decades of claims otherwise. Train the quadriceps through full range and it comes with it.

structures.name: Hamstrings
structures.action: Bend the knee and extend the hip.
structures.clinical: Injuries happen while lengthening under load, not while shortening — which is why Nordic curls protect and hamstring curls largely do not.

structures.name: Popliteus
structures.action: Unlocks the fully straight knee by rotating the shin inward.
structures.clinical: Small, deep and easily missed. A source of vague back-of-knee pain, particularly in downhill running.

structures.name: Patellar Tendon
structures.action: Connects the kneecap to the shin and transmits all quadriceps force.
structures.clinical: Jumper's knee. Isometrics reduce pain for hours; heavy slow loading and decline work rebuild it. Rest alone reliably fails.

structures.name: Quadriceps Tendon
structures.action: Connects the quadriceps to the top of the kneecap.
structures.clinical: Less common than patellar tendon problems but managed identically. Tenderness sits above the kneecap rather than below.

structures.name: Anterior Cruciate Ligament
structures.action: Stops the shin sliding forward on the thigh and controls rotation.
structures.clinical: Most injuries are non-contact, on landing or cutting with the knee collapsing inward. Landing mechanics and hop control are the prevention and the return-to-sport gate.

structures.name: Posterior Cruciate Ligament
structures.action: Stops the shin sliding backward on the thigh.
structures.clinical: Usually injured by a direct blow to the front of a bent knee — a dashboard or a fall onto the shin. Quadriceps strength is the mainstay of management.

structures.name: Medial Collateral Ligament
structures.action: Resists the knee being forced inward.
structures.clinical: The most commonly injured knee ligament and the one that heals best without surgery. Protect from sideways load early, then load progressively.

structures.name: Lateral Collateral Ligament
structures.action: Resists the knee being forced outward.
structures.clinical: Injured less often and heals less readily than the medial side. The common fibular nerve runs close by — check for foot drop.

structures.name: Menisci
structures.action: Wedge-shaped cartilage spreading load across the joint surface.
structures.clinical: Degenerative tears are common and often incidental on scan. Loading and strengthening outperforms surgery for most non-locking presentations.

structures.name: Pes Anserinus
structures.action: Shared attachment of three muscles on the inner shin below the knee.
structures.clinical: Tender inner knee pain, often confused with a medial meniscus or MCL problem but sitting lower and more superficial.

structures.name: Tibiofemoral Joint
structures.action: The main knee joint — hinging, with a small amount of rotation.
structures.clinical: The last few degrees of straightening matter more than the last few of bending. Lose full extension and every step costs more.

structures.name: Patellofemoral Joint
structures.action: Where the kneecap tracks in its groove on the thigh bone.
structures.clinical: Pain on stairs, hills and prolonged sitting. The problem is usually above and below — hip control and foot position — rather than at the kneecap itself.

structures.name: Vastus Lateralis
structures.action: The largest quadriceps head, on the outside of the thigh.
structures.clinical: Blends with the IT band, so tightness here contributes to the lateral pull on the kneecap. Frequently the dominant head, and the one that tracks the kneecap outward.

structures.name: Vastus Medialis
structures.action: The inner quadriceps head, running down to the inside of the kneecap.
structures.clinical: Wastes visibly and fast after knee swelling — compare the two thighs a hand's width above the kneecap and the difference is usually obvious.

structures.name: Vastus Intermedius
structures.action: Lies directly on the femur beneath rectus femoris.
structures.clinical: Not palpable — you are always feeling rectus femoris over it. Its deepest fibres form articularis genus, which pulls the joint capsule clear as the knee straightens.

structures.name: Biceps Femoris, Long Head
structures.action: Runs from the sitting bone to the head of the fibula. Crosses both hip and knee.
structures.clinical: The most commonly strained hamstring, and almost always at the top where the muscle meets tendon. Crossing two joints is why it fails during the reaching phase of a sprint stride.

structures.name: Biceps Femoris, Short Head
structures.action: Arises from the femur itself and crosses only the knee.
structures.clinical: The only hamstring part supplied by the common fibular nerve rather than the tibial — which is why it can be spared or affected independently of the others.

structures.name: Semitendinosus
structures.action: Runs from the sitting bone to the inside of the shin as a long cord-like tendon.
structures.clinical: Its tendon is prominent and easily felt behind the inner knee. Commonly harvested for ACL reconstruction, which leaves a measurable deficit in deep knee flexion strength.

structures.name: Semimembranosus
structures.action: The deepest and broadest hamstring, running to the back of the inner shin.
structures.clinical: Lies under semitendinosus, so tenderness felt deep to that cord is usually this. Its attachment is a common site of persistent posterior knee pain in runners.

structures.name: Plantaris
structures.action: A small muscle with a very long thin tendon running from the back of the knee to the heel.
structures.clinical: Absent in roughly one person in ten. Its rupture produces sudden sharp pain in the calf — the classic tennis leg — which mimics a serious calf tear but recovers far better.

structures.name: Patella
structures.action: The kneecap. A bone embedded within the quadriceps tendon.
structures.clinical: It exists to increase the leverage of the quadriceps, moving the tendon away from the joint centre. Its tracking depends on what pulls it — quadriceps balance above, hip control further up, foot position below.

structures.name: Proximal Tibiofibular Joint
structures.action: A small joint just below and outside the knee where the fibula meets the shin bone.
structures.clinical: Moves with every ankle movement, so a stiff one produces outer knee pain that changes with walking rather than with knee bending. The common fibular nerve wraps immediately below it.

structures.name: Gastrocnemius
structures.action: The upper calf. Points the foot down and crosses the knee.
structures.clinical: Because it crosses the knee, it must be tested with the knee straight. Restriction here caps ankle bending and pushes the problem up to the knee and hip.

structures.name: Gastrocnemius, Medial Head
structures.action: The larger inner head, from the medial femoral condyle.
structures.clinical: Where tennis leg happens — a sudden tear at the musculotendinous junction, felt as a blow to the calf. Larger and more often injured than the lateral.

structures.name: Gastrocnemius, Lateral Head
structures.action: The smaller outer head, from the lateral femoral condyle.
structures.clinical: Sits over the popliteal artery, which matters in the rare popliteal entrapment presentation in young athletes.

structures.name: Soleus
structures.action: The deep calf, lying under gastrocnemius and not crossing the knee.
structures.clinical: The real workhorse of walking and standing, and it limits ankle bending more than the upper calf does. Almost never trained directly — the seated calf raise is how you reach it.

structures.name: Achilles Tendon
structures.action: The strongest tendon in the body, joining both calf muscles to the heel bone.
structures.clinical: Midportion and insertional problems load differently — insertional cases often worsen with heel drops below neutral. Ask where it hurts before choosing the exercise.

structures.name: Tibialis Posterior
structures.action: The main dynamic support of the arch, turning the foot inward and pointing it down.
structures.clinical: Its failure is the usual cause of a progressively flattening adult foot. Inability to perform a single leg heel raise is the classic sign.

structures.name: Tibialis Anterior
structures.action: Pulls the foot up and controls its lowering to the ground after heel strike.
structures.clinical: Works eccentrically with every step. Central to shin splints, and its weakness is why tired runners slap their feet down.

structures.name: Fibularis Longus & Brevis
structures.action: Run down the outside of the shin and turn the foot outward.
structures.clinical: The primary active defence against rolling the ankle. Priority after any lateral sprain, and routinely under-dosed.

structures.name: Flexor Hallucis Longus
structures.action: Bends the big toe and contributes to push-off.
structures.clinical: Symptomatic in dancers and sprinters, and behind some persistent inner-ankle pain. Test it with the big toe extended.

structures.name: Plantar Fascia
structures.action: Thick band along the sole, tensioning the arch as the big toe extends at push-off.
structures.clinical: Worst with the first steps in the morning. Because big toe extension tensions it, limited big toe range is a frequent and overlooked driver.

structures.name: Intrinsic Foot Muscles
structures.action: Small muscles within the foot that hold the arch and fine-tune balance.
structures.clinical: Weak in almost anyone who has worn supportive shoes for decades. The foot's local stabilisers, and the equivalent of deep neck flexors or multifidus.

structures.name: Talocrural Joint
structures.action: The main ankle hinge — pointing the foot up and down.
structures.clinical: Bending range is the single most useful ankle measurement. Restriction here pushes compensation up into the knee and hip on every squat and stair.
structures.modelNote: The model carries no separate capsule mesh for the ankle joint — the ligaments shown are its collaterals, each also mapped individually.

structures.name: Subtalar Joint
structures.action: Sits below the ankle and handles side-to-side foot movement on uneven ground.
structures.clinical: Stiffens after ankle sprains and gets missed because everyone tests bending range instead. Heel bone work is what reaches it.

structures.name: First MTP Joint
structures.action: The big toe joint, which must extend roughly 60 degrees for a normal step.
structures.clinical: Restriction here alters every step and drives compensation up the whole chain. One of the most commonly missed causes of foot, knee and hip complaints.

structures.name: Lateral Ankle Ligaments
structures.latin: ligg. talofibulare anterius, talofibulare posterius et calcaneofibulare
structures.action: Resist the ankle rolling outward at the outside of the joint.
structures.clinical: The classic sprain. Roughly a third of people develop ongoing instability, almost always because balance and eversion work was stopped once the pain settled.

structures.name: Fibularis Longus
structures.action: Runs the length of the outer shin, then crosses under the foot to the base of the big toe.
structures.clinical: The only muscle that crosses the sole transversely, which makes it a genuine arch support and the reason it matters in flat foot as well as in ankle sprain.

structures.name: Fibularis Brevis
structures.action: Runs to the base of the fifth metatarsal on the outside of the foot.
structures.clinical: Its attachment is avulsed in the classic fifth metatarsal base fracture from an inversion sprain. Tenderness at that bony prominence after a rolled ankle needs imaging, not exercise.

structures.name: Sole, First Layer
structures.action: The most superficial layer — abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi.
structures.clinical: Abductor hallucis is the one that matters. It sits directly under the arch and is the main active support for it, and it is directly trained by short foot work.

structures.name: Sole, Second Layer
structures.action: Quadratus plantae and the lumbricals, working with the long toe flexor tendons.
structures.clinical: Quadratus plantae straightens the pull of the long flexor tendon so the toes curl in line rather than diagonally. Weakness here contributes to hammer toe.

structures.name: Sole, Third Layer
structures.action: Flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis and flexor digiti minimi brevis, concentrated at the front of the sole.
structures.clinical: Adductor hallucis pulls the big toe toward the others, so it is directly implicated in bunion progression. Toe splay work opposes it.

structures.name: Sole, Fourth Layer
structures.action: The interossei, deepest in the foot, spreading and closing the toes.
structures.clinical: The foot's equivalent of the hand interossei but far weaker in most people, because shoes remove the demand entirely.

structures.name: Flexor Digitorum Longus
structures.action: Runs down the back of the calf and behind the inner ankle to bend the four small toes.
structures.clinical: Passes through the tarsal tunnel with the tibial nerve. Claw-toe posture at rest often reflects it overworking to compensate for weak intrinsics.

structures.name: Extensor Hallucis Longus
structures.action: Lifts the big toe and assists pulling the foot upward.
structures.clinical: Its strength is the single most useful test for an L5 nerve root problem — weakness of big toe extension with everything else intact is a specific finding.

structures.name: Extensor Digitorum Longus
structures.action: Lifts the four small toes and helps pull the foot upward.
structures.clinical: Its tendons are visible fanning across the top of the foot. Works with tibialis anterior to clear the toes during the swing phase of a stride.

structures.name: Fibularis Tertius
structures.action: A small muscle that lifts the foot and turns it outward.
structures.clinical: Absent in a minority of people, so a missing tendon is a variant rather than a finding. Contributes to the combined lift-and-evert action that resists an inversion sprain.

structures.name: Extensor Digitorum Brevis
structures.action: A small muscle on the top of the foot assisting toe extension.
structures.clinical: Its fleshy belly on the outer top of the foot is commonly mistaken for swelling after an ankle sprain. Comparing both feet resolves it in seconds.

structures.name: Deltoid Ligament
structures.action: A broad fan of ligament on the inner ankle resisting the foot rolling outward.
structures.clinical: Far stronger than the outer ankle ligaments and much less often injured. When it is injured the ankle usually broke first — an inner ankle sprain deserves more suspicion than an outer one.

structures.name: Spring Ligament
structures.action: A thick band under the arch supporting the head of the talus from below.
