structures.clinical: The passive counterpart to tibialis posterior. When that tendon fails this ligament takes the load and eventually gives, which is the point at which a flexible flat foot becomes a fixed one.

structures.name: Tarsal Tunnel
structures.action: A passage behind the inner ankle carrying the tibial nerve, tendons and vessels into the sole.
structures.clinical: Produces burning in the sole that is often mistaken for plantar fasciitis. The distinguishing feature is night symptoms — plantar fascia pain is worst on the first steps of the morning and eases with movement.

structures.name: Extensor Retinaculum of the Ankle
structures.action: Bands across the front of the ankle holding the extensor tendons down.
structures.clinical: Compression here from tightly laced boots or ski boots produces numbness across the top of the foot and is entirely resolved by changing the lacing.

structures.name: Retrocalcaneal Bursa
structures.action: A fluid sac between the heel bone and the Achilles tendon.
structures.clinical: Tender on squeezing either side of the tendon just above the heel, which distinguishes it from tendon pain felt in the tendon itself. Aggravated by rigid heel counters.

structures.name: Sinus Tarsi
structures.action: A funnel-shaped space on the outside of the foot between the heel bone and the talus.
structures.clinical: Persistent tenderness in the soft dimple in front of the outer ankle bone after a sprain, worse on uneven ground. Dense with position sensors, which is part of why balance is disrupted long after a sprain has stopped hurting.

structures.name: Anterior Talofibular Ligament
structures.action: Runs forward from the front edge of the outer ankle bone to the neck of the talus.
structures.clinical: The first structure torn in an inversion sprain and the most commonly injured ligament in the body. Weakest of the three, and taut in plantarflexion — which is why the ankle rolls when the foot is pointed. Tenderness in the hollow just in front of the outer ankle bone.

structures.name: Calcaneofibular Ligament
structures.action: Runs down and back from the tip of the outer ankle bone to the heel bone, crossing both the ankle and the joint below it.
structures.clinical: The second to go, and the only lateral ligament crossing the subtalar joint — so its injury produces the rotational instability the ATFL alone does not. Taut with the foot flat, which is why testing it needs a neutral ankle.
structures.modelNote: The source model draws this ligament as a flat placeholder that never reaches the calcaneus. It is redrawn in the export by rule, from the tip of the lateral malleolus down and back to the lateral wall of the calcaneus. The shape is a schematic band, not a dissected structure.

structures.name: Posterior Talofibular Ligament
structures.action: Runs backward and inward from the inner surface of the outer ankle bone to the back of the talus.
structures.clinical: The strongest of the three and rarely injured in isolation. Its involvement means the ankle dislocated or came close, so a suspected PTFL injury deserves imaging before loading.

structures.name: Posterior Tibiotalar Ligament
structures.action: The deepest part of the deltoid, from the inner ankle bone back to the talus.
structures.clinical: The strongest component and the deep layer of the deltoid. Its rupture is what makes a medial ankle injury a surgical question rather than a rehab one.

structures.name: Tibiocalcaneal Ligament
structures.action: Runs straight down from the inner ankle bone to the sustentaculum tali on the heel.
structures.clinical: The longest superficial part, and the main restraint against the heel rolling outward. Loaded in the collapsing flat foot alongside tibialis posterior.

structures.name: Tibionavicular Ligament
structures.action: The most forward part, from the inner ankle bone to the navicular.
structures.clinical: Blends with the spring ligament below it. The two together are the passive arch support, which is why a failing spring ligament and a stretched deltoid appear as one problem.

structures.name: Anterior Talocalcaneal Ligament
structures.action: Runs from the neck of the talus down to the top of the heel bone.
structures.clinical: Part of the floor of the sinus tarsi. Contributes to the persistent tenderness in that hollow after a sprain.

structures.name: Lateral Talocalcaneal Ligament
structures.action: Runs down and back from the outer talus to the outer heel bone, parallel to the calcaneofibular ligament.
structures.clinical: Injured alongside the calcaneofibular ligament in a harder inversion sprain, and part of why subtalar movement stays stiff long after the ankle stops hurting.

structures.name: Medial Talocalcaneal Ligament
structures.action: Runs from the inner talus to the sustentaculum tali.
structures.clinical: Sits alongside the tibial nerve's course into the tarsal tunnel, so subtalar stiffness and inner-ankle nerve symptoms often travel together.

structures.name: Posterior Talocalcaneal Ligament
structures.action: Runs from the back of the talus down to the top of the heel bone.
structures.clinical: Sits in the same crowded space as the flexor hallucis longus tendon and the posterior talar process — the anatomy behind posterior ankle impingement in dancers.

structures.name: Distal Tibiofibular Syndesmosis
structures.action: Binds the two leg bones together just above the ankle, via the anterior, posterior and transverse tibiofibular ligaments.
structures.clinical: The high ankle sprain. Injured by forced outward rotation rather than inversion, tender above the joint line rather than below it, and it takes roughly twice as long to recover. Mistaking one for a lateral sprain is the single most common reason an ankle does not settle on schedule.

structures.name: Anterior Tibiofibular Ligament
structures.action: Runs down and out from the front of the tibia to the front of the fibula, just above the ankle.
structures.clinical: The first and most commonly injured part of the syndesmosis. Tender directly over it above the joint line, and the structure loaded by the squeeze and external rotation tests. Its isolated injury is the mildest high ankle sprain.

structures.name: Posterior Tibiofibular Ligament
structures.action: The posterior counterpart, from the back of the tibia to the back of the fibula.
structures.clinical: Considerably stronger than the anterior. Its involvement means a more significant injury, and its avulsion is the posterior malleolar fracture.

structures.name: Transverse Tibiofibular Ligament
structures.action: Deep to the posterior ligament, running across the back of the ankle.
structures.clinical: Effectively deepens the socket at the back, acting as a labrum for the talus. Rarely identified in isolation but part of why posterior syndesmotic injuries are slow.

structures.name: Bifurcate Ligament
structures.action: A Y-shaped ligament from the front of the heel bone splitting to the navicular and the cuboid.
structures.clinical: Avulses in an inversion sprain and produces tenderness in front of the outer ankle that is routinely misread as an ATFL injury. Point tenderness further forward, over the sinus tarsi rather than in front of the malleolus, distinguishes it.

structures.name: Short Plantar Ligament
structures.action: Runs from the front underside of the heel bone to the cuboid, deep to the long plantar ligament.
structures.clinical: With the long plantar ligament it supports the lateral arch. Relevant in lateral midfoot pain that plantar fascia work does not touch, and it forms part of the tunnel carrying the fibularis longus tendon.

structures.name: Dorsal Talonavicular Ligament
structures.action: Crosses the top of the joint between the talus and the navicular.
structures.clinical: Loaded when the foot is forced into plantarflexion. Dorsal midfoot tenderness after a sprain that is not the sinus tarsi is often this.

structures.name: Dorsal Calcaneocuboid Ligament
structures.action: Crosses the top of the joint between the heel bone and the cuboid.
structures.clinical: Part of the outer column of the midfoot. Tender in cuboid syndrome, where the cuboid sits slightly displaced and produces lateral foot pain with a normal X-ray.

structures.name: Anterior Longitudinal Ligament
structures.action: A broad band down the front of the vertebral bodies, the full length of the spine.
structures.clinical: The main passive brake on extension. Injured in hyperextension and in whiplash, and it is why an extension-based programme needs a screen first.

structures.name: Posterior Longitudinal Ligament
structures.action: Runs down the back of the vertebral bodies, inside the spinal canal.
structures.clinical: Narrows as it descends, leaving the lower lumbar discs least supported posterolaterally. That is precisely where herniations go, and why they press on the nerve root rather than straight back.

structures.name: Ligamentum Flavum
structures.action: Elastic bands joining adjacent vertebral arches, forming the back wall of the canal.
structures.clinical: The most elastic tissue in the body, and it thickens and buckles inward with age. A major contributor to spinal stenosis, which is why those patients feel better bent forward.

structures.name: Supraspinous Ligament
structures.action: Runs along the tips of the spinous processes.
structures.clinical: Directly palpable in the midline furrow. Tenderness on the tips rather than either side points here rather than at the facets.

structures.name: Interspinous Ligaments
structures.action: Fill the gaps between adjacent spinous processes.
structures.clinical: Loaded in flexion. A recognised source of midline low back pain in people who sit or bend for long periods.

structures.name: Nuchal Ligament
structures.action: The upward continuation of the supraspinous ligament, a sheet from the skull to C7.
structures.clinical: Trapezius, rhomboid minor and splenius all attach to it, so it is a shared anchor rather than a passive band. Palpable as the firm midline ridge at the back of the neck.

structures.name: Costotransverse Ligaments
structures.action: Bind each rib to the transverse process of its vertebra.
structures.clinical: Short and strong, so rib movement at this joint is small. Sharp mid-back pain that catches on a deep breath frequently sits here.

structures.name: Coraco-acromial Ligament
structures.action: Spans the coracoid to the acromion, completing the arch over the shoulder joint.
structures.clinical: Forms the roof of the subacromial space with the acromion. The cuff passes beneath it, so this ligament defines the space impingement happens in.

structures.name: Acromioclavicular Ligament
structures.action: Reinforces the top of the joint between collarbone and acromion.
structures.clinical: The first structure to fail in a fall onto the point of the shoulder. Isolated injury gives tenderness without a step deformity.

structures.name: Coracoclavicular Ligament
structures.action: Two bands — conoid and trapezoid — slinging the collarbone to the coracoid.
structures.clinical: What actually suspends the arm from the collarbone. Its rupture is what produces the visible step of a higher-grade separation, not the AC ligament alone.

structures.name: Transverse Humeral Ligament
structures.action: Bridges the two tubercles, roofing the bicipital groove.
structures.clinical: Holds the long head of biceps in its groove. When it fails the tendon subluxes, producing a painful snap with rotation.

structures.name: Sternoclavicular Ligaments
structures.action: Anterior and posterior bands plus the interclavicular band across the top.
structures.clinical: This joint almost never dislocates because of them. Anterior chest pain reproduced by pressing here is joint, not cardiac.

structures.name: Costoclavicular Ligament
structures.action: Binds the collarbone down to the first rib.
structures.clinical: Defines the costoclavicular space the nerve bundle passes through. A depressed shoulder narrows it — the reason a heavy bag reproduces arm symptoms.

structures.name: Superior Transverse Scapular Ligament
structures.action: Bridges the notch at the top of the scapula, turning it into a foramen.
structures.clinical: The suprascapular nerve passes under it while the vessels pass over. That makes this small ligament the roof of the first suprascapular entrapment site.

structures.name: Ulnar Collateral Ligament of the Elbow
structures.action: A triangular band on the inner elbow resisting valgus force.
structures.clinical: The Tommy John ligament. Its anterior band takes the load of a throw, and repetitive valgus stress is what fails it. Medial elbow pain in a thrower is this until proven otherwise.

structures.name: Radial Collateral Ligament of the Elbow
structures.action: Fans from the lateral epicondyle to the annular ligament, resisting varus force.
structures.clinical: Its posterolateral portion resists rotatory instability. Injured in elbow dislocation, and blends with the common extensor origin — which is why tennis elbow and ligament pain overlap.

structures.name: Ligament of the Head of the Femur
structures.action: Runs from the acetabular notch to a pit on the femoral head, carrying a small artery.
structures.clinical: Contributes little to stability in adults but its artery matters in children. Tears are a recognised cause of deep hip pain and clicking in dancers and gymnasts.

structures.name: Obturator Membrane
structures.action: Closes the large hole in the front of the pelvis, leaving a small canal at the top.
structures.clinical: The obturator nerve and vessels pass through that canal. It is where obturator nerve entrapment produces exercise-related groin pain.

structures.name: Oblique Popliteal Ligament
structures.action: An expansion of the semimembranosus tendon crossing the back of the knee.
structures.clinical: The main restraint against hyperextension. Tenderness deep in the popliteal fossa with pain on forced straightening points here.

structures.name: Arcuate Popliteal Ligament
structures.action: Arches over popliteus at the back-outer corner of the knee.
structures.clinical: Part of the posterolateral corner. Injury there is easily missed and, left untreated, is the commonest reason a cruciate reconstruction fails.

structures.name: Popliteofibular Ligament
structures.action: Runs from the popliteus tendon to the fibular head.
structures.clinical: With the arcuate ligament and LCL it forms the posterolateral corner. Combined external rotation and varus laxity is the pattern.

structures.name: Transverse Ligament of the Knee
structures.action: Joins the front horns of the two menisci.
structures.clinical: Links their movement, so the menisci translate together during bending. Occasionally mistaken for a tear on imaging where it meets the meniscus.

structures.name: Interosseous Membrane of the Leg
structures.action: A fibrous sheet between tibia and fibula along their length.
structures.clinical: Transfers load between the two bones and separates the front and back compartments. Its upper opening carries the anterior tibial vessels — relevant in anterior compartment syndrome.

structures.name: Long Plantar Ligament
structures.action: The longest ligament in the foot, from the heel bone forward to the metatarsal bases.
structures.clinical: The deepest passive support of the lateral arch, and it forms a tunnel for the fibularis longus tendon. Relevant in lateral midfoot pain that plantar fascia work does not touch.

structures.name: Fibular Retinacula
structures.action: Bands holding the fibularis tendons behind and below the outer ankle.
structures.clinical: When the superior band fails the tendons snap forward over the bone — a painful click on the outside of the ankle, often after a sprain and frequently misdiagnosed as instability.

structures.name: Deep Transverse Metatarsal Ligament
structures.action: Joins the heads of the metatarsals across the front of the foot.
structures.clinical: The digital nerves pass beneath it. Compression there is Morton's neuroma — burning between the third and fourth toes, eased by removing the shoe.

structures.name: Intersesamoid Ligament
structures.action: Joins the two small bones beneath the big toe joint.
structures.clinical: Part of the plantar plate complex. Turf toe is a tear of this complex from forced big toe extension, and it needs protection from that range rather than mobilisation into it.

structures.name: Lateral Temporomandibular Ligament
structures.action: Thickened capsule on the outer side of the jaw joint.
structures.clinical: The only true ligament of the TMJ, and the main brake on the jaw dropping backward and down. It is what limits opening range when the joint is guarded.

structures.name: Sphenomandibular Ligament
structures.action: Runs from the sphenoid bone to the inner surface of the mandible.
structures.clinical: Acts as a swinging hinge for the jaw. Considered a passive restraint rather than a treatment target, but it explains why the mandible arcs as it does on opening.

structures.name: Stylohyoid Ligament
structures.action: From the styloid process behind the ear down to the hyoid bone.
structures.clinical: Can calcify with age. When it does, turning the head produces throat or ear pain — Eagle syndrome, rare but real, and worth knowing before treating it as muscular.

structures.name: Deltoid Fascia
structures.action: Invests the deltoid, continuous with the pectoral fascia in front and the infraspinatus fascia behind.
structures.clinical: Sends septa between the three parts of the deltoid, which is part of why they can act independently.

structures.name: Pectoral Fascia
structures.action: Covers pectoralis major and continues into the axilla.
structures.clinical: Continuous with the deltoid fascia laterally and the abdominal fascia below — one reason chest tightness and abdominal bracing patterns travel together.

structures.name: Clavipectoral Fascia
structures.action: A deep sheet from the collarbone enclosing subclavius and pectoralis minor.
structures.clinical: The nerve bundle passes behind it. A short pectoralis minor tightens this sheet, which is a mechanism for arm symptoms independent of the muscle itself.

structures.name: Brachial Fascia
structures.action: Sleeves the upper arm and sends septa dividing front from back compartments.
structures.clinical: Those septa are where the radial and ulnar nerves cross between compartments — fixed points at which a nerve can be tethered.

structures.name: Antebrachial Fascia
structures.action: Sleeves the forearm, thickening at the wrist into the retinacula.
structures.clinical: Its thickening forms the roof of the carpal tunnel, so forearm fascia and carpal tunnel are one continuous structure rather than two.

structures.name: Fascia Lata
structures.action: The fascial sleeve of the thigh, thickened laterally into the iliotibial tract.
structures.clinical: Gluteus maximus and TFL both insert into it, so it is how those muscles act on the knee at all. Treating the IT band without them is treating the rope, not the pull.

structures.name: Crural Fascia
structures.action: Sleeves the lower leg and divides it into four compartments.
structures.clinical: It does not stretch, which is why swelling inside a compartment raises pressure rather than expanding. The anatomical basis of compartment syndrome.

structures.name: Popliteal Fascia
structures.action: Roofs the diamond-shaped hollow behind the knee.
structures.clinical: A Baker's cyst pushes against it, which is why the swelling is felt as firm and localised rather than diffuse.

structures.name: Masseteric Fascia
structures.action: Covers masseter, continuous with the fascia over temporalis above.
structures.clinical: Continuity with the temporal fascia is one route by which jaw tension and temple headache travel together.

structures.name: Temporal Fascia
structures.action: A tough sheet over temporalis, from the temporal line down to the zygomatic arch.
structures.clinical: Dense and unyielding, so temporalis has no room to swell. Part of why the muscle refers so readily into the temple.

structures.name: Transversalis Fascia
structures.action: Lines the inner surface of the abdominal wall, deep to transversus abdominis.
structures.clinical: Forms the deep ring of the inguinal canal. Its weakness is the anatomical basis of a direct inguinal hernia.

structures.name: Iliopsoas Fascia
structures.action: Envelops psoas and iliacus from the lumbar spine to the lesser trochanter.
structures.clinical: The femoral nerve runs within it. A tight or thickened sheath is one explanation for anterior thigh symptoms with a normal-looking hip.

structures.name: Anserine Bursa
structures.action: Sits between the pes anserinus tendons and the tibia, about four fingers below the inner knee joint line.
structures.clinical: Pes anserine bursitis — inner knee pain below the joint line, worse on stairs and getting out of a car, and common in runners and in knee osteoarthritis. Tenderness below the joint line rather than on it is what separates it from a medial meniscus problem.

structures.name: Semimembranosus Bursa
structures.action: Lies between the semimembranosus tendon and the medial head of gastrocnemius at the back of the knee.
structures.clinical: This is where a Baker's cyst forms — it communicates with the joint, so the cyst is usually a symptom of something inside the knee rather than a problem in itself. Treating the cyst without asking why the knee is producing fluid misses the point.

structures.name: Prepatellar Bursae
structures.action: Three bursae in front of the kneecap — subcutaneous, subfascial and subtendinous.
structures.clinical: Housemaid's knee. Swelling sits in front of the kneecap and the joint itself moves freely, which distinguishes it from an effusion. Caused by kneeling, so the intervention is a kneeling pad before anything else.

structures.name: Infrapatellar Bursae
structures.action: Superficial and deep bursae either side of the patellar tendon below the kneecap.
structures.clinical: The deep one is implicated in jumper's knee alongside the tendon. Tenderness either side of the tendon rather than on it points at the bursa.

structures.name: Subdeltoid Bursa
structures.action: Continuous with the subacromial bursa, extending beneath the deltoid.
structures.clinical: Usually one continuous space with the subacromial bursa, which is why pain referred into the outer arm is so common with impingement. Tenderness extending well below the acromion is this part.

structures.name: Iliopectineal Bursa
structures.action: The largest bursa in the body, between the iliopsoas tendon and the front of the hip.
structures.clinical: Communicates with the hip joint in around one person in seven. Deep groin pain with an audible or palpable snap on moving from flexion to extension is internal snapping hip, and this bursa is why it hurts.

structures.name: Subcutaneous Calcaneal Bursa
structures.action: Sits between the skin and the Achilles tendon at the back of the heel.
structures.clinical: The superficial one, distinct from the retrocalcaneal bursa in front of the tendon. Caused by shoe pressure, so it responds to footwear rather than to loading. Tender on pinching the skin over the tendon.

structures.name: Coracohumeral Ligament
structures.action: Runs from the coracoid to both humeral tubercles, roofing the rotator interval.
structures.clinical: The primary restraint against inferior translation with the arm at the side, and it thickens and contracts in frozen shoulder. Loss of external rotation with the arm at the side is its signature — earlier and more specific than loss of abduction.

structures.name: Pubofemoral Ligament
structures.action: Runs from the pubic part of the acetabular rim to the front of the femoral neck.
structures.clinical: Limits abduction and extension. Tight, it caps the hip abduction a wide stance or a Cossack squat needs, and the compensation shows up at the low back.

structures.name: Transverse Acetabular Ligament
structures.action: Bridges the notch at the bottom of the socket, completing the labral ring.
structures.clinical: Turns the labrum from a horseshoe into a closed ring, which is what lets the joint hold a vacuum seal. Loss of that seal is part of why labral tears produce a feeling of instability rather than only pain.

structures.name: Radiate Ligament of the Head of the Rib
structures.action: Fans from the head of each rib onto the two vertebral bodies it spans and the disc between them.
structures.clinical: Each rib is anchored to two vertebrae and the disc between, which is why a single rib cannot move without loading two spinal segments. The anatomy behind sharp, well-localised mid-back pain that catches on a breath.

structures.name: Patellar Retinacula
structures.action: Fibrous expansions either side of the kneecap from the vastus muscles.
structures.clinical: A tight lateral retinaculum tips the kneecap outward and is a genuine contributor to patellofemoral pain — one of the few structures around the kneecap you can actually change by hand.

structures.name: Dorsal Radiocarpal Ligament
structures.action: Runs obliquely across the back of the wrist from the radius to the triquetrum.
structures.clinical: Resists the carpal bones sliding forward. Injured in a fall onto a bent wrist, and a contributor to dorsal wrist pain that persists after the fracture question is settled.

structures.name: Pisohamate & Pisometacarpal Ligaments
structures.action: Extend forward from the pisiform to the hook of the hamate and the fifth metacarpal.
structures.clinical: Effectively the continuation of the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon, and they form the floor and ulnar wall of Guyon's canal. That is why handlebar pressure on the pisiform compresses the ulnar nerve.

structures.name: Rhomboid Major
structures.action: The larger, lower rhomboid, from T2–T5 to the medial scapular border below the spine.
structures.clinical: The bulk of what people feel as the ache between the shoulder blades. Its length, not its strength, is usually the problem.

structures.name: Rhomboid Minor
structures.action: The smaller, upper rhomboid, from C7–T1 to the medial border at the scapular spine.
structures.clinical: Sits under the upper trapezius and blends with the nuchal ligament above. Frequently part of what feels like a stubborn upper trapezius that will not release.

structures.name: Articularis Genus
structures.action: A few slips of muscle from the deep quadriceps to the top of the knee joint capsule.
structures.clinical: Pulls the capsule clear of the joint as the knee straightens, so it does not get pinched. Its failure after immobilisation contributes to the loss of terminal extension that quad work alone does not restore.

structures.name: Cranium
structures.action: The skull without the lower jaw. Eight bones forming the brain case and fourteen forming the face.
structures.clinical: The sutures between them fuse with age but retain a small amount of movement throughout life. The pterion, where four bones meet at the temple, is the thinnest part of the skull.

structures.name: Clavicle
structures.action: The collarbone. The only long bone lying horizontally, and the sole bony strut connecting the arm to the trunk.
structures.clinical: The first bone to begin forming in the fetus and the last to finish. Its S-shape and subcutaneous position make it the most commonly fractured bone in the body.

structures.name: Humerus
structures.action: The upper arm bone, from the shoulder socket to the elbow.
structures.clinical: The radial nerve spirals around its back in a groove, which is why a mid-shaft fracture produces wrist drop. The axillary nerve wraps its neck, which is why dislocation produces numbness over the outer shoulder.

structures.name: Radius
structures.action: The forearm bone on the thumb side. It rotates around the ulna to turn the palm.
structures.clinical: Its lower end is the most commonly fractured site in the body from a fall onto an outstretched hand. Its head at the elbow is where a pulled elbow slips out of its ligament ring.

structures.name: Ulna
structures.action: The forearm bone on the little-finger side. It forms the main hinge of the elbow and stays relatively still during rotation.
structures.clinical: Almost entirely subcutaneous along its length, so it is followed easily from the point of the elbow to the wrist. It carries the elbow; the radius carries the wrist.

structures.name: Carpal Bones
structures.action: Eight small bones in two rows of four forming the wrist.
structures.clinical: The scaphoid bridges both rows and takes the load from a fall, which is why it fractures most and heals worst — its blood supply enters from the far end, so a fracture can cut off the near half.

structures.name: Metacarpals and Phalanges
structures.action: Five metacarpals in the palm and fourteen finger bones, with two in the thumb rather than three.
structures.clinical: The thumb's metacarpal joint is a saddle shape allowing movement in every direction, which is what makes opposition possible and is also why it wears out.

structures.name: Hip Bone
structures.action: Three bones — ilium, ischium and pubis — fused into one during adolescence.
structures.clinical: The three meet in the hip socket itself, so a growth plate injury there in a young athlete is a different problem from an adult hip injury.

structures.name: Sacrum and Coccyx
structures.action: Five fused vertebrae forming the back of the pelvis, ending in three to five small fused coccygeal bones.
structures.clinical: The spinal cord ends around L1 but nerve roots continue through the sacral canal. The coccyx retains some movement and is a genuine source of pain after a fall onto it.

structures.name: Femur
structures.action: The thigh bone. The longest and strongest bone in the body.
structures.clinical: Its neck angles inward from the shaft, and that angle governs how load transfers into the pelvis. Too steep or too shallow changes hip mechanics for a lifetime.

structures.name: Tibia
structures.action: The shin bone. Carries essentially all the weight from knee to ankle.
structures.clinical: Its front border is entirely subcutaneous, which is why shin injuries hurt disproportionately and why stress fractures there are so tender to direct pressure.

structures.name: Fibula
structures.action: The slender outer leg bone. Carries almost no weight but stabilises the ankle.
structures.clinical: Bears under a tenth of the load, which is why sections of it can be removed as bone graft. Its lower end forms the outer ankle and is essential to ankle stability even though it carries no weight.

structures.name: Tarsal Bones
structures.action: Seven bones forming the back half of the foot — talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid and three cuneiforms.
structures.clinical: The talus has no muscle attachments at all; it is moved entirely by the bones around it. Its blood supply is precarious, so talar fractures risk the bone dying.

structures.name: Metatarsals and Phalanges
structures.action: Five metatarsals and fourteen toe bones forming the front half of the foot.
structures.clinical: The second metatarsal is the longest and most rigidly fixed, which is why it takes most stress fractures in runners and marchers.

structures.name: Atlanto-Occipital Joint
structures.action: Where the skull sits on the first vertebra. Produces nodding — flexion and extension only.
structures.clinical: The yes joint. Restriction here shows up as a chin that pokes forward on nodding because the movement is coming from lower down instead.

structures.name: Atlantoaxial Joint
structures.action: Where the first vertebra pivots on the peg of the second. Produces rotation.
structures.clinical: The no joint, and roughly half of all neck rotation happens here. Test it in full flexion, which locks the levels below. Instability here is a genuine concern in rheumatoid arthritis and Down syndrome.

structures.name: Uncovertebral Joints
structures.action: Small joints at the upper side edges of the cervical vertebral bodies, unique to the neck.
structures.clinical: They form after childhood rather than being present from birth. Bony spurs here narrow the exit hole for the nerve root, which is a common cause of arm symptoms in older patients.

structures.name: Sternocostal Joints
structures.action: Where the upper seven rib cartilages meet the breastbone.
structures.clinical: Costochondritis sits here — chest pain reproduced exactly by pressing on the joint. That reproducibility is what distinguishes it from cardiac pain and is worth demonstrating to an anxious patient.

structures.name: Sacrococcygeal Joint
structures.action: Where the coccyx meets the bottom of the sacrum.
structures.clinical: Moves during sitting and childbirth. Coccydynia after a fall or delivery is real and often dismissed — sitting on one buttock or on a wedge cushion is the most effective single change.

structures.name: Intercarpal Joints
structures.action: The many small joints between the eight wrist bones, contributing collectively to wrist movement.
structures.clinical: Wrist movement is distributed across two rows rather than happening at one joint. That is why a stiff wrist rarely has one restriction, and why weight-bearing progressions restore range better than stretching does.

structures.name: Finger Joints
structures.action: The knuckle joints and the two joints in each finger.
structures.clinical: Knuckles are loosest straight and tightest bent, which is why a hand splinted straight stiffens badly. Any hand held still should be positioned with the knuckles bent.

structures.name: Metatarsophalangeal Joints
structures.action: The joints at the base of the toes, where the foot pivots at push-off.
structures.clinical: The big toe joint needs around sixty degrees of extension for a normal step. Restriction there is one of the most commonly missed drivers of foot, knee and hip complaints.

structures.name: Mastoid Process
structures.action: The bony bump directly behind the earlobe.
structures.clinical: The single most useful upper cervical landmark. Almost everything that rotates or side-bends the head attaches here or just behind it.

structures.name: External Occipital Protuberance
structures.action: The bump in the midline at the back of the skull, level with the top of the ears.
structures.clinical: The midline reference for suboccipital work. Trace laterally from here along the ridge to find the whole suboccipital attachment line.

structures.name: Superior Nuchal Line
structures.action: The ridge running sideways from the occipital bump toward each mastoid process.
structures.clinical: Where the suboccipitals, upper trapezius and semispinalis all attach. Tenderness anywhere along it is the most common physical finding in cervicogenic headache.

structures.name: Transverse Process of C1
structures.action: A small bony point in the hollow between the mastoid process and the jaw angle.
structures.clinical: The widest cervical transverse process and the only one reachable from the side. Press gently — the vertebral artery runs close by, and it is tender in almost everyone.

structures.name: Spinous Process of C2
structures.action: The first large bump you meet moving down the midline from the base of the skull.
structures.clinical: The anchor for counting cervical levels, and the attachment for the deepest suboccipitals. Its rotation under your thumb during head turn tells you how C1 on C2 is moving.

structures.name: Vertebra Prominens (C7)
structures.action: The most prominent bump at the base of the neck.
structures.clinical: The starting point for counting down the spine. Distinguish it from T1 by feeling while the head turns — C7 moves, T1 stays put.

structures.name: Angle of the Mandible
structures.action: The corner of the jaw, below and in front of the earlobe.
structures.clinical: Masseter attaches on the outside and medial pterygoid on the inside of this same corner — the two mirror each other across the bone, which is why jaw work often needs both.

structures.name: Zygomatic Arch
structures.action: The bony bridge running from the cheekbone back toward the ear.
structures.clinical: Masseter hangs from it and temporalis runs beneath it. Following the arch backward leads directly to the jaw joint.

structures.name: Acromion
structures.action: The flat bony shelf forming the point of the shoulder.
structures.clinical: The roof of the subacromial space. Palpating just under its front edge with the arm extended behind reaches the supraspinatus tendon.

structures.name: Coracoid Process
structures.action: A finger-shaped projection about two centimetres below the outer end of the collarbone, felt in the hollow below it.
structures.clinical: Three muscles attach to one small point — pectoralis minor, coracobrachialis and the short head of biceps. Universally tender, so tenderness alone means little.

structures.name: Spine of the Scapula
structures.action: The horizontal ridge across the back of the shoulder blade, continuous with the acromion.
structures.clinical: Divides supraspinatus above from infraspinatus below. Its medial end sits level with the T3 spinous process — a useful cross-check when counting thoracic levels.

structures.name: Inferior Angle of the Scapula
structures.action: The bottom point of the shoulder blade.
structures.clinical: Sits level with T7. The easiest single point for tracking shoulder blade position and for feeling upward rotation as the arm rises.

structures.name: Medial Border of the Scapula
structures.action: The inner edge of the shoulder blade running vertically beside the spine.
structures.clinical: Where people point when they say the pain is between the shoulder blades. Rhomboids attach along it and serratus anterior wraps around its front surface.

structures.name: Greater Tubercle of the Humerus
structures.action: The bony prominence on the outer top of the arm bone, just below and lateral to the acromion.
structures.clinical: Three of the four cuff tendons converge here. Rolling the arm outward brings supraspinatus forward under your fingers.

structures.name: Bicipital Groove
structures.action: A vertical channel on the front of the upper arm bone, found by rolling the arm gently in and out under your thumb.
structures.clinical: Carries the long head of biceps. Tenderness here in an overhead athlete points at the biceps tendon rather than the cuff — but the groove is tender in most people, so compare sides.

structures.name: Jugular Notch
structures.action: The hollow at the top of the breastbone between the two collarbones.
structures.clinical: Sits level with the T2 and T3 disc. The starting point for finding the sternoclavicular joints, one on each side.

structures.name: Sternal Angle
structures.action: The ridge partway down the breastbone where its top section meets the body.
structures.clinical: The second rib attaches here, which makes it the reference for counting ribs — the only reliable way to number them. Sits level with the T4 and T5 disc behind.

structures.name: Costal Margin
structures.action: The lower border of the ribcage, sloping down and out from the bottom of the breastbone.
structures.clinical: Where the diaphragm attaches all the way round. Its movement under your hands during breathing tells you whether someone is breathing into their ribs or their neck.

structures.name: Medial Epicondyle of the Humerus
structures.action: The bony bump on the inner side of the elbow.
structures.clinical: Golfer's elbow. The ulnar nerve runs in a groove immediately behind it — tapping there produces tingling into the little finger, and that groove is a treatment site as much as the tendon in front of it.

structures.name: Lateral Epicondyle of the Humerus
structures.action: The bony bump on the outer side of the elbow.
structures.clinical: Tennis elbow, though the tender point is usually a centimetre distal on the ECRB tendon rather than on the bone itself. Tenderness further down again suggests the radial nerve through supinator instead.

structures.name: Olecranon
structures.action: The point of the elbow.
structures.clinical: With the elbow bent, it forms a triangle with the two epicondyles. Loss of that triangle after trauma suggests dislocation. A swelling directly over it is olecranon bursitis, which sits on top of the bone rather than in the joint.

structures.name: Radial Styloid Process
structures.action: The bony point on the thumb side of the wrist.
structures.clinical: Sits about a centimetre further down than the ulnar styloid — a difference that disappears in a Colles fracture. The de Quervain's tendons cross directly over it.

structures.name: Ulnar Styloid Process
structures.action: The bony point on the little-finger side of the wrist.
structures.clinical: The cartilage complex sits just distal to it. Tenderness in the hollow between this and the pisiform is the classic finding in ulnar-sided wrist pain.

structures.name: Anatomical Snuffbox
structures.action: The hollow at the base of the thumb, deepest when the thumb is lifted away from the hand.
structures.clinical: The scaphoid sits in its floor. Tenderness here after a fall onto an outstretched hand means a scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise — and it often does not show on an initial X-ray.

structures.name: Pisiform
structures.action: A pea-sized bone felt on the little-finger side of the palm at the wrist crease.
structures.clinical: The entrance to Guyon's canal sits immediately beside it. In cyclists with hand numbness, this is where the handlebar pressure lands.

structures.name: Iliac Crest
structures.action: The top rim of the pelvis, followed easily with both hands resting on the hips.
structures.clinical: Its highest point sits level with the L4 spinous process — the standard way to count lumbar levels. The superior cluneal nerves cross it about seven centimetres from the midline.

structures.name: Anterior Superior Iliac Spine
structures.action: The bony point at the front of the pelvis, at the front end of the iliac crest.
structures.clinical: The primary reference for pelvic position and for comparing leg length. The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve passes just medial to it — the reason a belt sitting here produces burning on the outer thigh.

structures.name: Posterior Superior Iliac Spine
structures.action: The bony point at the back of the pelvis, found under the dimples above the buttocks.
structures.clinical: Sits level with the second sacral segment and marks the sacroiliac joint. Comparing the two sides against the ASIS is the standard pelvic position assessment.

structures.name: Ischial Tuberosity
structures.action: The sitting bone, easiest to find with the hip bent.
structures.clinical: All three hamstrings and part of adductor magnus attach here. Deep pain worse on sitting on a hard chair and worse with stretching is high hamstring tendinopathy — which needs loading, not stretching.

structures.name: Greater Trochanter
structures.action: The broad bony prominence on the outside of the hip, about a hand's width below the iliac crest.
structures.clinical: The most commonly tender lateral hip landmark. Gluteus medius and minimus attach to distinct facets on it — the tendinopathy is usually at the medius facet, slightly behind and above the most obvious point.

structures.name: Pubic Tubercle
structures.action: A small bony point either side of the midline at the front of the pelvis.
structures.clinical: The adductor longus tendon attaches immediately below it, which is where a groin strain is felt. The inguinal ligament ends here. Explain before palpating.

structures.name: Sacral Base
structures.action: The flat top surface of the sacrum, felt just below the L5 spinous process.
structures.clinical: The transition between the mobile lumbar spine and the fixed pelvis, and therefore a concentration point for load. The step down from L5 to sacrum is palpable and exaggerated in spondylolisthesis.

structures.name: Tibial Tuberosity
structures.action: The bump on the front of the shin a few centimetres below the kneecap.
structures.clinical: Where the patellar tendon attaches. Enlarged and tender in adolescents with Osgood-Schlatter, which is a growth plate traction problem and settles with skeletal maturity.

structures.name: Gerdy's Tubercle
structures.action: A small flat area on the outer shin, level with and lateral to the tibial tuberosity.
structures.clinical: Where the IT band attaches. Tenderness here is distal IT band pain, distinct from the far more common pain at the outer femoral condyle a few centimetres higher.

structures.name: Knee Joint Line
structures.action: The horizontal gap between thigh bone and shin, easiest to find with the knee bent to ninety degrees.
structures.clinical: Tenderness along it is the most reproducible physical sign of a meniscal problem. The medial and lateral collateral ligaments cross it at either end.

structures.name: Head of the Fibula
structures.action: The bony knob on the outside of the leg, just below and behind the knee joint line.
structures.clinical: The common fibular nerve wraps around the bone immediately below it, where it is the most superficial nerve in the leg. Crossed legs, plaster casts and a fall onto the outer knee all compress it there.

structures.name: Adductor Tubercle
structures.action: A small bony point at the top of the inner knee, just above the femoral condyle.
structures.clinical: Where the hamstring portion of adductor magnus attaches. A reliable reference for finding the adductor canal, which runs just above and in front of it.

structures.name: Medial Malleolus
structures.action: The bony bump on the inside of the ankle.
structures.clinical: Sits higher and further forward than the outer one. The tarsal tunnel runs immediately behind it, carrying the tibial nerve and the tibialis posterior tendon into the sole.

structures.name: Lateral Malleolus
structures.action: The bony bump on the outside of the ankle.
structures.clinical: Lower and further back than the inner one. The anterior talofibular ligament runs forward from its front edge and is the first structure torn in an inversion sprain.

structures.name: Navicular Tuberosity
structures.action: A bony prominence on the inner border of the foot, roughly midway between the inner ankle bump and the big toe joint.
structures.clinical: The main attachment of tibialis posterior, and the keystone of the inner arch. Its height off the floor between sitting and standing is a simple measure of how much the arch drops under load.

structures.name: Base of the Fifth Metatarsal
structures.action: The prominent bump on the outer border of the midfoot.
structures.clinical: Fibularis brevis attaches here and can avulse it during an inversion sprain. Tenderness at this point after a rolled ankle needs imaging before any loading.

structures.name: Sustentaculum Tali
structures.action: A small shelf on the heel bone, felt about a thumb's width directly below the inner ankle bump.
structures.clinical: Supports the talus from below and anchors the spring ligament. A precise reference point for locating the subtalar joint and for heel bone mobilisation.

structures.name: Cervical Nerve Roots
structures.action: Emerge from the neck between vertebrae and form the nerve supply to the arm.
structures.clinical: Root irritation follows a band down the arm rather than a nerve's own territory. Lateral glide is usually the gentlest and safest place to start.

structures.name: Brachial Plexus
structures.action: The nerve bundle running from the neck, between the scalenes and under the collarbone, into the arm.
structures.clinical: Arm symptoms often trace here rather than to the shoulder. Three narrow points along its path — between the scalenes, under the collarbone, and beneath pectoralis minor.

structures.name: Median Nerve
structures.action: Supplies most of the forearm flexors and sensation to the thumb, index and middle fingers.
structures.clinical: Compressible at the neck, at pronator teres, and at the wrist. Symptoms at the wrist do not mean the problem is at the wrist — check all three.

structures.name: Ulnar Nerve
structures.action: Runs behind the inner elbow and supplies the little and ring fingers.
structures.clinical: Most exposed at the elbow, where prolonged bending compresses it — hence symptoms on waking or after a long phone call. Provokes very easily; dose the glides low.

structures.name: Radial Nerve
structures.action: Wraps behind the upper arm and supplies the extensors and the back of the hand.
structures.clinical: Can mimic tennis elbow closely. If elbow loading is not progressing as expected, test the nerve before adding more load.

structures.name: Lumbosacral Plexus
structures.action: The nerve network in the low back and pelvis supplying the whole leg.
structures.clinical: Leg symptoms that do not follow one nerve's territory usually originate here rather than peripherally.

structures.name: Sciatic Nerve
structures.action: The largest nerve in the body, running from the low back through the buttock and down the back of the leg.
structures.clinical: Passes beneath piriformis, and through it in a minority. Sliders before tensioners always — and symptoms travelling further down the leg means stop, not push.

structures.name: Femoral Nerve
structures.action: Runs down the front of the thigh, supplying the quadriceps and the front of the leg.
structures.clinical: Front-of-thigh symptoms are much less commonly recognised than sciatic ones and are frequently misread as a quadriceps or hip flexor strain.

structures.name: Common Fibular Nerve
structures.action: Wraps around the outside of the knee just below the joint, supplying the outer shin and top of the foot.
structures.clinical: The most superficial nerve in the leg and the easiest to compress — crossed legs, a tight cast, a fall onto the outer knee. Foot drop is the red flag.

structures.name: Tibial Nerve
structures.action: Runs down the back of the calf and behind the inner ankle into the sole.
structures.clinical: Compression behind the inner ankle produces burning in the sole, often mistaken for plantar fasciitis. The distinguishing feature is night symptoms.

structures.name: Spinal Accessory Nerve
structures.action: Supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. The only cranial nerve to supply a large limb-girdle muscle.
structures.clinical: Runs superficially across the back triangle of the neck with almost no protection, which is why lymph node biopsy is the classic cause of injury. Presents as a drooping shoulder, trapezius wasting and difficulty raising the arm overhead.

structures.name: Greater Occipital Nerve
structures.action: Sensory nerve from the C2 level supplying the back of the scalp up to the crown.
structures.clinical: Pierces semispinalis capitis and trapezius on its way up — both are compression sites. Produces a sharp or burning headache from the base of the skull over the back of the head, often mistaken for migraine. Tender on pressure just below the skull line.

structures.name: Phrenic Nerve
structures.action: Arises from C3, C4 and C5 and is the sole motor supply to the diaphragm.
structures.clinical: C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive. Because it starts in the neck, diaphragm irritation refers to the shoulder tip — a patient with unexplained shoulder-top pain and no shoulder findings deserves a second thought.

structures.name: Trigeminal Nerve
structures.action: Sensation to the face, and via its lower branch the motor supply to all four chewing muscles.
structures.clinical: Trigeminal neuralgia is sharp, electric, one-sided facial pain triggered by light touch, chewing or wind. That presentation needs medical assessment, not manual therapy — jaw work is for muscular jaw pain, which is a different problem entirely.

structures.name: Facial Nerve
structures.action: Supplies every muscle of facial expression, plus platysma, stylohyoid and the back belly of digastric.
structures.clinical: Bell's palsy is sudden one-sided facial weakness including the forehead. Forehead sparing points to a stroke instead and is a medical emergency. Facial retraining is a specialist field and not homecare exercise.
structures.noExercises: Facial nerve rehabilitation is specialist neuromuscular retraining, outside the scope of this library. Refer rather than prescribe.

structures.name: Dorsal Scapular Nerve
structures.action: Supplies levator scapulae and both rhomboids.
structures.clinical: Pierces the middle scalene, which makes a tight scalene a genuine compression site. Produces a deep ache along the inner border of the shoulder blade that resists surface work because the source is in the neck.

structures.name: Long Thoracic Nerve
structures.action: Supplies serratus anterior. Arises from C5, C6 and C7 and runs a long superficial course down the side of the ribcage.
structures.clinical: Its length and exposure make it the most commonly injured nerve in this group — carrying a heavy bag, a blow to the ribs, or sustained overhead work. Produces a winged scapula and an inability to raise the arm fully overhead.

structures.name: Suprascapular Nerve
structures.action: Supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
structures.clinical: Two narrow points along its path — the notch at the top of the shoulder blade and a second behind the joint. Compression at the second spares supraspinatus, so isolated infraspinatus wasting with intact abduction strength points here rather than at the cuff.

structures.name: Axillary Nerve
structures.action: Supplies deltoid and teres minor, plus sensation over the outer shoulder.
structures.clinical: Wraps the surgical neck of the humerus and passes through a small gap behind the joint. Vulnerable in shoulder dislocation and in fractures of the upper humerus. Numbness over the shoulder badge area after a dislocation is the sign to check for.

structures.name: Musculocutaneous Nerve
structures.action: Supplies coracobrachialis, biceps and brachialis, then continues as sensation to the outer forearm.
structures.clinical: Pierces coracobrachialis, which is a compression site in heavy overhead athletes. Weak elbow flexion with a normal grip, plus numbness along the outer forearm, is the pattern.

structures.name: Thoracodorsal Nerve
structures.action: Supplies latissimus dorsi.
structures.clinical: Runs down the back wall of the armpit. Most often injured during axillary surgery. Rarely a manual therapy finding, but worth knowing when lat strength is unexpectedly and one-sidedly poor.

structures.name: Pectoral Nerves
structures.action: Supply pectoralis major and minor.
structures.clinical: The medial branch passes through pectoralis minor. A short pec minor therefore compresses both this nerve and the neurovascular bundle behind it, which is why pec minor length matters more than its strength.

structures.name: Intercostal Nerves
structures.action: Twelve pairs running in a groove under each rib, supplying the intercostals and the abdominal wall.
structures.clinical: Run in a protected groove on the underside of each rib, which is why rib fractures and post-surgical scars produce persistent band-like pain around the chest. Pain following one rib line rather than a broad area points here.

structures.name: Superior Cluneal Nerves
structures.action: Sensory branches from the upper lumbar levels crossing the top of the pelvis to supply the skin over the buttock.
structures.clinical: Cross the iliac crest through a tight fibrous tunnel roughly seven centimetres from the midline. Entrapment there produces low back and buttock pain indistinguishable from a facet or disc problem — and it responds to belts and waistbands rather than to spinal work. Genuinely underdiagnosed.

structures.name: Obturator Nerve
structures.action: Supplies the adductor group and sensation to the inner thigh.
structures.clinical: Passes through a canal at the front of the pelvis. Compression there produces groin pain that worsens with exercise and eases with rest — a recognised and frequently missed cause of persistent groin pain in kicking and change-of-direction athletes.

structures.name: Superior Gluteal Nerve
structures.action: Supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae.
structures.clinical: Injury produces a dropping pelvis on the unsupported side when standing on one leg. Classically iatrogenic from badly placed injections into the buttock — which is why the upper outer quadrant is the only safe site.

structures.name: Inferior Gluteal Nerve
structures.action: Supplies gluteus maximus.
structures.clinical: Injury makes rising from a chair and climbing stairs difficult while walking on the flat stays normal. That specific pattern separates it from general hip weakness.

structures.name: Lateral Femoral Cutaneous Nerve
structures.action: Purely sensory to the outer thigh. Passes under the inguinal ligament near the front of the hip bone.
structures.clinical: Meralgia paraesthetica — burning, numbness or hypersensitivity over the outer thigh with no weakness at all. Caused by tight belts, low-rise waistbands, tool belts, body armour, pregnancy or weight gain. The most effective intervention is usually removing the compression, not exercise.

structures.name: Saphenous Nerve
structures.action: The longest sensory branch of the femoral nerve, running down the inside of the thigh, knee and shin.
structures.clinical: Compressed where it exits a tunnel in the inner thigh. Produces inner knee pain with no joint findings, frequently misattributed to the medial meniscus or the pes anserinus. Purely sensory, so strength is always normal.
